p1a.label: Paper 1 (a) — interpretation impression
p1a.template: What impression does the author give about …? You must use Extract X to explain your answer.
p1a.asks: Work out the overall impression (the author's view or tone) about the named issue, then prove it with two pieces of the extract's wording or detail and explain what each shows.
steps: Read the question focus and underline it.
Read the extract twice; decide the overall impression in a few words (e.g. 'well-organised and controlled').
Pick two short quotations or details that create that impression.
For each: quote it, then explain how the word choice or detail creates the impression.
Finish with one sentence restating the impression.
p1a.plan: About 8 minutes: 1 minute deciding the impression, 6 minutes writing, 1 minute checking you used the extract.
success: States a clear impression that answers the question
Supports it with selected words or details from the extract
Explains how those details create the impression (analysis of the author's language/choice of detail)
mistakes: Summarising the extract instead of identifying an impression
Bringing in lots of own knowledge — this question rewards analysis of the extract
Quoting long passages without explaining them

full: The author gives the impression that …
Firstly, the extract says “…”, which suggests that …
Also, the author describes … as “…”, which shows …
Therefore, the impression the author gives is that …
some: Impression
Quote 1 + what it suggests
Quote 2 + what it shows
Restate the impression

model.t: The author gives the impression that life in Nazi Germany was extremely well-organised and controlled.
model.n: Topic sentence with the impression stated (department model).

model.t: Firstly, the extract describes people who “marched in neat rows at the rally”, which suggests the Nazis created a disciplined and united image.
model.n: Quotation + explanation of what the detail suggests.

model.t: Therefore, the impression the author gives is that Nazi Germany appeared united, disciplined and loyal to Hitler.

p1a.model_note: Adapted from the Arcadia IGCSE model paragraphs. The quoted words illustrate the technique; they are not from a real published extract.

markscheme.source: Paraphrased from the 4HI1/01 June 2025 mark scheme (generic levels for (a)). Check the wording against your copy, then tick verified.

levels.descriptor: A simple impression is identified, with little or no support from the extract.
An impression is identified and supported with some relevant detail from the extract, with some analysis of how it is created.
The impression is clearly analysed, supported by well-selected detail from the extract, showing how the author's choices create it.

strong: Pick ONE clear impression, then explain HOW the author creates it — word choice, tone, emphasis, choice of evidence, or what is left out (e.g. a Rosa Parks extract that ignores Claudette Colvin).
weak: Identifying an impression and quoting supporting evidence only — this stays in Level 2.
Listing several impressions instead of developing one.

p1b.label: Paper 1 (b) — explain two effects
p1b.asks: Explain two different consequences of the event. Each needs precise knowledge and an explanation of how the event led to that effect.
steps: Underline the event and what it affected (e.g. 'on the Nazi Party').
Choose two clearly different effects.
Paragraph 1: name the effect, give precise evidence (date, number, name, law), explain how the event caused it.
Paragraph 2: same pattern for a second effect.
Keep each paragraph on 'effect' — not a story of the event.
p1b.plan: About 12 minutes: 1 minute planning two effects, 5 minutes per paragraph, 1 minute checking.
success: Each supported with accurate, specific knowledge
Each explained — how the event led to the effect
mistakes: Writing only one effect (the mark scheme caps this at 4 marks, with no access to Level 3)
Describing the event instead of its effects
Two effects that are really the same point

full: One important effect of … was … For example, … As a result, …
Another important effect of … was … For instance, … This meant that …
some: Effect 1: name it + evidence + 'as a result'
Effect 2: name it + evidence + 'this meant'

model.t: One important effect of the Wall Street Crash was mass unemployment.
By 1932 over 6 million Germans were unemployed.
As a result, many people lost faith in the Weimar government because it seemed unable to solve the crisis.

p1b.model_note: From the Arcadia IGCSE model paragraphs. A full answer needs a second effect in the same pattern.

markscheme.source: Paraphrased from the 4HI1/01 June 2025 mark scheme (generic levels for (b)). Check, then tick verified.

levels.descriptor: A simple or generalised answer, lacking development; limited knowledge of the topic.
Features of the period are analysed to explain at least one effect; some accurate and relevant knowledge supports it. Maximum 4 marks if only one effect is explained.
Two effects are explained with developed analysis; accurate and relevant knowledge shows good understanding. Level 3 is not available if only one effect is explained.

markscheme.notes: One effect only: maximum 4 marks, no access to Level 3.

strong: Explain HOW the issue led to each effect, and say what the effect was on.
Accurate, specific knowledge (e.g. effects of the Reichstag Fire on Nazi power; effects of Watergate on trust in the presidency).
weak: Knowing the effect but not explaining the link.
General detail without specific examples.

p1c.label: Paper 1 (c) — how far do you agree
p1c.template: ‘[Statement].’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer. You may use the following in your answer: [two prompts]. You must also use information of your own.
p1c.asks: Weigh the factor in the statement against others and reach a supported judgement. You must go beyond the two prompts with at least one point of your own.
steps: Underline the factor in the statement and the dates.
Plan three paragraphs: the stated factor, the second prompt, and one point of your own.
Open with your judgement ('To a large/some/limited extent …').
Write each paragraph: point, precise evidence, explanation, link back to the statement.
Conclude by comparing the factors using a criterion (e.g. which lasted longest, affected most people, caused the most change).
p1c.plan: About 24 minutes: 3 minutes planning three aspects, 18 minutes writing, 3 minutes conclusion and check.
success: Covers three aspects including one beyond the prompts
Analysis explains how each aspect relates to the statement
Clear judgement with a reason in the conclusion
mistakes: Only using the two prompts (caps the mark: Level 2 max 6, Level 3 max 10, no Level 4)
Describing instead of explaining how the factor mattered
Ending without a judgement or with 'they were all important'

full: Introduction: I agree to a large / some / limited extent that … because …
The most significant reason … was … Firstly, in [date], … This meant that … This was highly significant because …
However, another important reason was … For example, … This shows that …
Furthermore, [your own point] … For instance, … As a result, …
Overall, … was the most important because it lasted longest / affected the most people / caused the biggest change, whereas …
some: Judgement
Factor in the statement
Second prompt
Your own point
Conclusion using a criterion

model.t: The most significant reason life was difficult for German Jews was the impact of the Nuremberg Laws.
Firstly, in 1935 these laws banned marriages between Jews and non-Jews and stripped Jews of German citizenship.
This meant that Jews were legally excluded from German society and lost protection under the law.
This was highly significant because it created long-term legal discrimination, so the Nuremberg Laws were a turning point because they made discrimination official government policy.

p1c.model_note: Adapted from the Arcadia IGCSE model paragraphs (last sentence lightly corrected).

markscheme.source: Paraphrased from the 4HI1/01 June 2025 mark scheme (generic levels for (c)). Check, then tick verified.

levels.descriptor: A simple or generalised answer with limited analysis; limited knowledge; judgement asserted.

An explanation is given, showing limited analysis and organisation; some accurate knowledge; an overall judgement is given but its justification is undeveloped. Maximum 6 marks if it does not go beyond the aspects in the prompts.

An explanation is given, showing some analysis, generally directed at the question; accurate and relevant knowledge; overall judgement given with some justification. Maximum 10 marks if it does not go beyond the prompts.

An analytical explanation directed consistently at the question; accurate, relevant knowledge used to support it; criteria for the judgement are justified and applied. Not available if the answer does not go beyond the prompts.

markscheme.notes: Three aspects needed (at least one beyond the prompts) to reach Level 4.

strong: Focus on the question’s issue, second-order concept (cause, consequence, significance) and date range from the first paragraph.
Judge at the end of each paragraph, then weigh the factors in the conclusion.
Analyse relative importance and how factors interacted (e.g. hyperinflation against Versailles, the Ruhr and constitutional weakness).
weak: Describing events without explaining how they caused the outcome.
Drifting outside the date range or the topic (e.g. into the Eastern Front for a home-front question; into how Hitler became Chancellor for a question on the Party’s growth to 1928).
Confusing groups (e.g. Catholics and Protestants).

p2ba.label: Paper 2 B (a) — explain two similarities or differences
p2ba.template: Explain TWO ways in which … was similar to / different from …
p2ba.asks: Compare two named situations or periods and explain two specific similarities or differences, with evidence from both sides of the comparison.
steps: Underline both things being compared and the dates.
Choose two clear similarities (or differences).
For each: state it, give evidence for BOTH sides, explain why that is a similarity/difference.
Keep it to two developed points — no introduction needed.
p2ba.plan: About 9 minutes: 1 minute choosing two points, 4 minutes per point.
success: Evidence from both sides of each comparison
mistakes: Describing one period, then the other, without comparing

full: One way in which … was different from … was … In [period 1], … whereas in [period 2], … This shows that …
A second difference was … In [period 1], … However, by [period 2], … Therefore …
some: Comparison 1: both sides + explanation
Comparison 2: both sides + explanation

markscheme.source: Paraphrased from the 4HI1/02 June 2025 mark scheme (breadth study (a)). Check, then tick verified.

levels.descriptor: Simple or generalised comment; limited knowledge.
Similarity/difference explained with some analysis and supporting knowledge. Maximum 3 marks if only one is explained.
Two similarities/differences explained with developed analysis, supported by accurate, relevant knowledge.

p2bb.label: Paper 2 B (b) — explain two causes
p2bb.asks: Explain two different reasons why something happened, each supported by precise evidence and an explanation of how it caused the outcome.
steps: Underline the outcome and the dates.
Choose two distinct causes.
For each: name the cause, give precise evidence, then explain how it led to the outcome ('As a result…').
Do not tell the story of the outcome itself.
p2bb.plan: About 12 minutes: 1 minute planning, 5 minutes per cause, 1 minute checking.
success: Clear explanation of how each caused the outcome
mistakes: Only one cause (maximum 4 marks, no Level 3)
Describing events without saying how they caused the outcome
Using a cause outside the date range

full: One important cause of … was … Firstly, in [date], … As a result, … because …
A second cause was … For example, … This led to … because …
some: Cause 1 + evidence + how it caused the outcome
Cause 2 + evidence + how it caused the outcome

markscheme.source: Paraphrased from the 4HI1/02 June 2025 mark scheme (breadth study (b)). Check, then tick verified.

levels.descriptor: Simple or generalised answer; limited knowledge.
At least one cause explained with some analysis and supporting knowledge. Maximum 4 marks for one cause.
Two causes explained with developed analysis, supported by accurate and relevant knowledge. Not available for one cause.

p2bc.label: Paper 2 B (c) — how far (themes)
p2bc.template: How far … in the years …? Explain your answer. You may use the following in your answer: [two prompts]. You must also use information of your own.
p2bc.asks: Make a judgement about change, continuity or the importance of a factor across a long period, using the two prompts and at least one point of your own from a different part of the period.
steps: Underline the concept (change, turning point, main reason) and the dates.
Plan three aspects spread across the date range — at least one beyond the prompts.
Open with a judgement.
In each paragraph, explain how far that aspect shows change (or importance), with precise evidence.
Conclude with a criterion-based judgement across the whole period.
p2bc.plan: About 24 minutes: 3 minutes planning, 18 minutes writing, 3 minutes conclusion and check.
success: Three aspects across the period, one beyond the prompts
mistakes: Covering only the start of the period
Only using the prompts (caps the mark)

full: To a large / some / limited extent … because …
Firstly, [prompt 1, with date] … This shows … because …
Secondly, [prompt 2] … However, … which suggests …
Furthermore, [own point from a different part of the period] …
Overall, … because [criterion: how much changed, how many people were affected, how long it lasted].
some: Judgement
Aspect 1
Aspect 2
Own aspect
Conclusion with criterion

model.t: The discovery of penicillin was a turning point to a large extent because it transformed the treatment of infection.
Firstly, Alexander Fleming identified penicillin in 1928, the first effective antibiotic. This shows that treatment could now kill bacteria rather than just manage symptoms.
Secondly, in the 1940s Florey and Chain developed ways to mass-produce penicillin, which saved thousands of lives during the Second World War.
model.n: Second piece of evidence, later in the period.

model.t: This was significant because it marked a permanent change in the treatment of disease, making bacterial infections curable rather than fatal.

p2bc.model_note: From the Arcadia IGCSE model paragraphs.

markscheme.source: Paraphrased from the 4HI1/02 June 2025 mark scheme (breadth study (c)). Check, then tick verified.

levels.descriptor: Simple or generalised answer with limited analysis; limited knowledge; judgement asserted.
Limited analysis and organisation; some accurate knowledge; judgement with undeveloped justification. Maximum 6 marks if it does not go beyond the prompts.
Some analysis directed at the question; accurate, relevant knowledge; judgement with some justification. Maximum 10 marks if it does not go beyond the prompts.
Analytical explanation consistently directed at the question; accurate knowledge supports it; justified criteria applied to the judgement. Requires going beyond the prompts.

p2aa.label: Paper 2 A (a) — describe two features
p2aa.template: Describe TWO features of EITHER [X] OR [Y].
p2aa.asks: Choose one of the two topics and describe two separate features of it, each with precise supporting detail. No explanation of importance is needed.
steps: Pick the option you know more about.
Identify two different features (things that happened or characteristics).
For each: a topic sentence naming the feature, then one or two precise supporting details.
Keep it short — this is a 6-mark describe question.
p2aa.plan: About 8 minutes: 1 minute choosing, 3–4 minutes per feature.
success: Each supported with accurate, specific detail
mistakes: Writing about both options instead of choosing one
Explaining causes or consequences at length instead of describing

full: One important feature was … Firstly, … This shows that …
Another important feature was … Secondly, … This meant that …
some: Feature 1 + detail
Feature 2 + detail

model.t: One important feature was the use of tunnels. The Vietcong built underground bases to hide fighters and supplies from US bombing.
model.n: Topic sentence with the feature + precise detail.

model.t: Another important feature was ambushes. Vietcong troops used booby traps such as punji sticks and carried out hit-and-run attacks, so US troops lived in constant fear of attack.

p2aa.model_note: Adapted from the Arcadia IGCSE model paragraphs.

markscheme.source: Paraphrased from the 4HI1/02 June 2025 mark scheme (Section A (a)). Check, then tick verified.

levels.descriptor: Simple or generalised comment; limited knowledge.
Features described with some supporting knowledge. Maximum 3 marks if only one feature is described.
Two features described, each supported by accurate and relevant knowledge.

strong: Signpost two separate features ("One feature… A second feature…").
Concise answers — Level 3 is reachable in well under a side.
weak: Over-long answers that waste time for the 16-mark question.

p2ab.label: Paper 2 A (b) — how far does Source A support Source B
p2ab.template: How far does Source A support the evidence of Source B about …? Explain your answer.
p2ab.asks: Compare what the two sources say about the named issue. Find where they agree and where they differ, quote both, and reach a judgement on how far A supports B.
steps: Underline the issue in the question.
Read both sources and highlight points on that issue only.
Paragraph 1: agreement — quote/paraphrase both sources.
Paragraph 2: difference — quote/paraphrase both sources.
Judgement: supports to a large / some / limited extent, with a reason (e.g. the main point agrees but details differ).
p2ab.plan: About 12 minutes: 2 minutes reading, 9 minutes writing, 1 minute judgement.
success: Identifies agreement between the sources, with reference to both
Identifies difference between the sources, with reference to both
Reaches a supported judgement on how far they agree
mistakes: Describing each source separately without comparing
Only finding agreement (or only difference) — both are needed for Level 2 and above
Bringing in lots of own knowledge or provenance — this question is about comparing content

full: Source A supports Source B to a large / some / limited extent.
Both sources suggest that … Source A says “…” and Source B shows “…”.
However, they differ because Source A says “…” whereas Source B …
Overall, Source A supports Source B … because …
some: Judgement
Agreement (both sources)
Difference (both sources)
Overall

markscheme.source: Paraphrased from the 4HI1/02 June 2025 mark scheme (Section A (b)). Check, then tick verified.

levels.descriptor: Simple comparison; limited reference to the sources.
Agreement and/or difference identified with some support from both sources. Agreement and difference must both be identified to reach 5 marks.
Agreement and difference explained with well-selected support from both sources; a judgement on the extent of support.

markscheme.notes: Both agreement and difference are needed for 5 marks or more.

strong: Show agreement AND difference, supported by quoting or paraphrasing both sources.
Judge the overall extent of support, including tone and overall message, not just details (e.g. both sources agreed Rolling Thunder caused damage but was not a complete success).
weak: Similarity and difference asserted without support.
Not explaining where the sources differ or what one source says that the other does not.
Commenting on reliability — it is not credited here.

p2ac.label: Paper 2 A (c) — how far do you agree with Extract C
p2ac.template: Extract C suggests that … How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use Extract C, Sources A and B and your own knowledge to explain your answer.
p2ac.asks: Evaluate the historian's interpretation in Extract C: test it against Sources A and B and your own knowledge, show where it is convincing and where it is not, and reach a judgement.
steps: Underline the interpretation in the question.
Explain what Extract C argues, quoting it.
Use Source A and/or B and own knowledge to SUPPORT the interpretation.
Use Source A and/or B and own knowledge to CHALLENGE it.
Judgement: how far you agree, and why.
p2ac.plan: About 25 minutes: 3 minutes reading and planning, 19 minutes writing, 3 minutes judgement.
success: Analyses the interpretation in Extract C
Uses Sources A and B to support and challenge it
Uses accurate own knowledge to test it
mistakes: Ignoring one of the sources or the extract
Using own knowledge as a separate story rather than to test the interpretation

full: To a large / some / limited extent, I agree that … Extract C states “…”.
Firstly, this is supported by Source A, which … My own knowledge also shows that …
However, Source B suggests … Furthermore, [own knowledge] …
Therefore, this interpretation is only partially / largely valid because …
some: Judgement + Extract C
Support (sources + knowledge)
Challenge (sources + knowledge)
Conclusion

model.t: To a large extent, Extract C is convincing when it states that bombing destroyed villages but not the spirit of the Vietcong.
model.n: Topic sentence with qualifier, using the extract.

model.t: Firstly, this is supported by Source A, which highlights how Vietcong fighters used guerrilla tactics and the Ho Chi Minh Trail to keep fighting despite US bombing.
model.n: Support from a source + own knowledge.

model.t: However, Source B emphasises that the South Vietnamese government was corrupt and unpopular, which meant the USA could not rely on strong allies. Therefore, the view is only partially valid: bombing was important, but political weakness in the South also played a decisive role.

p2ac.model_note: Adapted from the Arcadia IGCSE model paragraphs. The extract and source wording is illustrative, not from a real paper.

markscheme.source: Paraphrased from the 4HI1/02 June 2025 mark scheme (Section A (c)). Check, then tick verified.

levels.descriptor: Simple judgement on the interpretation; limited use of the extract, sources and knowledge.
Some analysis of the interpretation, with some use of the sources and knowledge to support or challenge it; judgement with limited support.
Analysis of the interpretation using the extract, sources and knowledge to support and challenge it; judgement with some justification.
Sustained evaluation of the interpretation, integrating the extract, both sources and precise knowledge; well-justified judgement.

strong: State a judgement early and sustain it.
Use the sources AND the extract AND own knowledge for both sides; use contradictory material in the counter-argument.
Notice subtleties in the extract (e.g. a US "victory" that was not a real success).
weak: One-sided answers or a source-by-source audit.
Using the extract to prove its own claim.
Leaving the judgement to a brief conclusion, or not concluding.

u1.label: Unit 1 essay — assess this view (interpretations)
u1.template: Historians differ in their judgements about … ‘[Statement].’ Assess this view using your own knowledge of the issue.
u1.asks: Treat the statement as one historian's interpretation. Explore it, explore the alternative views, and reach a substantiated judgement on which view is most convincing, using valid criteria.
steps: Plan (10 minutes): underline the stated view, the concept (cause, consequence, significance) and the dates. List the stated factor plus 2–3 alternatives.
Introduction: 'Some historians argue that … whilst others argue that …' Name your criteria (duration, scope, effectiveness, impact) and give your judgement.
Explore the stated view first, with precise evidence (statistics, key people, events, dates, acts/laws).
Make sure about half the essay explores other views — each paragraph weighs its factor against your criteria.
Link back to the wording of the question in every paragraph.
Conclusion: rank the factors and show why one view is more convincing than the others, using your criteria.
u1.plan: 60 minutes per essay: 10 minutes planning, about 45 minutes writing, 5 minutes checking. You answer two essays in 2 hours.
success: Strand 1 — key issues raised by the view are analysed and explored as issues of interpretation
Strand 2 — sufficient, accurate knowledge meets most of the question's demands
Strand 3 — valid criteria are established and applied to reach a supported overall judgement
mistakes: Not focusing on the exact view in the opening paragraph (examiners note this in Level 2 answers)
Considering other views only near the end of the essay
Narrative description of events instead of analysis of their importance
A conclusion that lists factors ('… was important too') without showing why one is more significant
Going outside the dates in the question

frames.name: Department factor-question frame
full: Introduction: Some historians argue that … Whilst others argue that … In assessing [topic], key criteria such as [duration / scope / effectiveness / impact] will be employed to argue that … [your judgement]

Not the most important factor: Despite my judgement, it could be argued that X was the most important … For example, … This meant that … (2–3 pieces of evidence) However, this argument is weak because … [against a criterion] Thus we must assert that …

Most important factor: In line with my judgement, … For example, … This meant that … (2–3 pieces of evidence) A dissenting view might point to … because … On the balance however, … Thus we must assert that …

Conclusion: In conclusion, I agree/disagree with the view that … The most important reason was … because … The second most important was … because … it is less important than the first because … The least important was … because …
some: Introduction: views + criteria + judgement
Factor not most important: point, evidence + impact ×2–3, weakness against criteria, sustain judgement
Most important factor: point, evidence + impact ×2–3, dissenting view, why it still wins, sustain judgement
Conclusion: ranked factors linked to criteria

criteria_list: Duration — which factor was important for the longest time?
Scope — which factor affected the most people or things?
Impact — which factor led to the most fundamental change?
u1.evidence_tip: When selecting evidence think SPEDA: statistics, key people, events, dates and acts/laws.
u1.frame_note: The department expects the factor-question frame: introduction with views and criteria (duration, scope, effectiveness, impact), paragraphs on weaker factors that weigh them against the criteria, a paragraph on the strongest factor with a dissenting view, and a conclusion that ranks factors and links back to the criteria. Evidence: statistics, key people, events, dates and acts/laws.

levels.descriptor: Simple or generalised statements are made about the view presented in the question. Some accurate and relevant knowledge is included, but it lacks range and depth and does not directly address the issue in the question. Judgement on the view is assertive, with little supporting evidence.

Some understanding of the issue raised by the question is shown and analysis is attempted by describing some points that are relevant. Mostly accurate knowledge is included, but it lacks range or depth and only has implicit links to issues relevant to the question. A judgement on the view is given, but with limited support and the criteria for judgement are left implicit.

Understanding and some analysis of the issue raised by the question is shown by selecting and explaining some key points of view that are relevant. Knowledge is included to demonstrate some understanding of the issues raised by the question, but material lacks range or depth. Although some of the evaluations may only be partly substantiated, the overall judgement is supported.

u2a.label: Section A (a) — value of a source
u2a.template: Why is Source 1 valuable to the historian for an enquiry into …? Explain your answer using the source, the information given about it and your own knowledge of the historical context.

Identify 2–3 developed inferences from the source that are relevant to the enquiry.

Use contextual knowledge to support AND challenge those claims.
Analyse author, purpose and audience — how do they shape reliability?
Distinguish fact from opinion.
Note significant omissions and why they matter.
End with a balanced overall judgement on the weight it can bear.

u3a.label: Section A — use two sources together
u3a.template: How far could the historian make use of Sources 1 and 2 together to investigate …? Explain your answer, using both sources, the information given about them and your own knowledge of the historical context.
u3a.asks: Judge how useful the two sources are, together, for the specific enquiry. Interrogate what each source shows (inference), test it against context, weigh the provenance, and explain how the sources complement or limit each other.
steps: Decode the enquiry (5 minutes): underline exactly what the historian is investigating and the dates.
Read both sources and their provenance; annotate who, when, why, for whom.
Source 1: make 2–3 developed inferences relevant to the enquiry; support or challenge each with precise context.
Source 2: the same, then show how it adds to, confirms or contradicts Source 1.
Evaluate weight: how do nature, purpose, audience and the author's position affect how far each can be trusted for this enquiry? Separate information from claim or opinion.
Judgement: how far the sources together can be used, and with what degree of certainty.
u3a.plan: About 60 minutes: 10 minutes reading and planning, 45 minutes writing, 5 minutes checking.
success: Interrogates both sources with reasoned inferences, separating information from claim or opinion
Uses precise contextual knowledge to illuminate and test the sources' limitations
Shows understanding of the values and concerns of the society the sources come from
Evaluates with justified criteria, weighing the evidence and the degree of certainty it supports
mistakes: Summarising or paraphrasing the sources instead of making inferences
Adding context as a separate block instead of applying it to the sources
Stereotypical provenance comments ('it's biased because he was there')
Treating the sources separately with no comment on using them together
Drifting into answering the history question instead of judging the sources

u3b.label: Section B — thematic essay across periods
u3b.template: ‘[Statement about two or more periods, or the whole period].’ How far do you agree with this statement?
u3b.asks: Make a sustained, criteria-based judgement across the named periods or themes. Compare periods and factors rather than treating each in isolation.
steps: Decode (3 minutes): underline the claim, the comparison and EVERY date range. Define what would make something 'main' or 'most significant'.
Plan (7 minutes): plan four PEEJ paragraphs — e.g. stated factor and alternative in period 1, then in period 2 — with two precise examples each.
Introduce (5 minutes): define the debate and criteria; give a provisional answer that can differ between periods.
Develop (about 32 minutes): four PEEJ paragraphs — specific evidence, its effect, and a comparative judgement at the end of each.
Conclude (8 minutes) and check (5 minutes): answer 'how far' across BOTH periods using your criteria; check dates and comparisons.

Valid criteria established, applied and weighed to reach the judgement
mistakes: Covering only one of the named periods, or drifting outside the dates
Narrating each period in turn without comparing them
Assuming every black American's experience was identical (most examples concern the South)
A conclusion that repeats evidence instead of weighing it with criteria

topics.title: The establishment of the Weimar Republic and its early problems

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Depth study 3, key topic 1. Read more: Payne, Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Germany, chapter 1 (pp. 2–23).

learn.intro: In November 1918 the Kaiser abdicated and Germany became a democracy. Within five years the new Weimar Republic faced a hated peace treaty, uprisings from left and right, a French invasion of the Ruhr and hyperinflation.

sections.title: 1. The Kaiser's abdication and the German Revolution, 1918–19

blocks.p: By autumn 1918 Germany was losing the war and its people were starving because of the British naval blockade. In late October sailors at Kiel mutinied rather than sail on a final mission. Workers' and soldiers' councils took control in many cities.

On 9 November 1918 Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated and fled to the Netherlands. Friedrich Ebert, leader of the Social Democrats (SPD), became head of government and a republic was declared. Two days later, on 11 November, the new government signed the armistice ending the fighting.
Elections in January 1919 chose a National Assembly. Because Berlin was dangerous, it met in the quiet town of Weimar — giving the Republic its name.

evidence: January 1919: National Assembly elected; meets at Weimar.

sections.title: 2. The Weimar Constitution: strengths and weaknesses

ul: Strength: very democratic — men and women over 20 could vote; the Reichstag was elected every four years.
Strength: a Bill of Rights guaranteed freedoms such as free speech and religion.
Weakness: proportional representation meant many small parties, so governments were coalitions that often collapsed.
Weakness: Article 48 let the President rule by decree in an emergency — later used to bypass the Reichstag.
Weakness: judges, army officers and civil servants from the Kaiser's time stayed in their jobs, and many disliked the Republic.

evidence: Votes for men and women over 20.
President elected every 7 years; Article 48 emergency powers.

sections.title: 3. Reactions to the Treaty of Versailles

blocks.p: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919. Germany lost about 13 per cent of its land, including Alsace-Lorraine and land given to Poland, and all its colonies. Its army was limited to 100,000 men, with no tanks, air force or submarines, and the Rhineland was demilitarised. Under the 'war guilt' clause (Article 231) Germany accepted blame for the war, and in 1921 reparations were set at £6,600 million.

Germans were furious. They called it a Diktat — a dictated peace — because they had not been allowed to negotiate. The politicians who signed it were called the 'November criminals', and many believed the 'stab in the back' myth that the army had been betrayed by politicians. The Republic was linked with humiliation from the start.

sections.title: 4. Challenges from the Left and Right

blocks.p: Left: in January 1919 the communist Spartacists, led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, tried to seize power in Berlin. Ebert used the army and the Freikorps — ex-soldiers who hated communism — to crush the rising. Luxemburg and Liebknecht were murdered.

Right: in March 1920 Wolfgang Kapp led Freikorps units into Berlin in the Kapp Putsch. The army refused to stop them and the government fled. Workers in Berlin called a general strike; with the city at a standstill, Kapp gave up within days.
Right-wing extremists also murdered politicians, including Matthias Erzberger (1921) and Foreign Minister Walther Rathenau (1922). Judges often gave right-wing offenders light sentences.

evidence: March 1920: Kapp Putsch defeated by a general strike.

sections.title: 5. The Ruhr occupation and hyperinflation, 1923

blocks.p: When Germany failed to make a reparations payment, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr, Germany's main industrial area, in January 1923, to take goods instead. The government told workers to use passive resistance — to go on strike — and kept paying them by printing more money.

Causes of hyperinflation: the government had already printed money to pay for the war; reparations drained gold and goods; the Ruhr occupation cut production while the government printed even more money. By November 1923 a loaf of bread cost about 200 billion marks.

Effects: savers, pensioners and people on fixed incomes were ruined; wages could not keep up with prices; some people bartered goods. But some gained: people who had borrowed money paid off debts cheaply, and some businessmen bought up property. Many middle-class Germans blamed the Republic.

evidence: January 1923: French and Belgian troops occupy the Ruhr.
November 1923: a loaf of bread cost about 200 billion marks.

learn.intro: After the chaos of 1923, Germany recovered. Gustav Stresemann stabilised the currency, reorganised reparations with American help and won back Germany's international standing. But how strong was the recovery?

sections.title: 1. Stresemann and the economy

blocks.p: Gustav Stresemann was Chancellor for a few months in 1923 and Foreign Minister from 1923 until his death in October 1929. In 1923 he called off passive resistance in the Ruhr and introduced a new temporary currency, the Rentenmark, in November 1923; it was replaced by the Reichsmark in 1924. Hyperinflation ended.

The Dawes Plan (1924): reparations payments were lowered to 1,000 million marks a year for the first five years, rising later to 2,500 million; the USA loaned Germany 800 million gold marks; and French and Belgian troops left the Ruhr. Over the next six years Germany received more than 25 billion marks in American loans, which paid for new factories, roads, housing and public buildings.

The Young Plan (1929) reduced the total reparations bill to around $8 billion, to be paid over 59 years. Nationalists including Hitler campaigned against it and collected 4 million signatures for a referendum, but it went ahead.

evidence: 1924: Dawes Plan — US loan of 800 million gold marks.
More than 25 billion marks of US loans over six years.
1929: Young Plan — around $8 billion over 59 years.

sections.title: 2. Successes abroad

ul: Locarno Treaties (1925): Germany accepted its western borders with France and Belgium. Germany was treated as an equal again.
League of Nations (1926): Germany joined and was given a permanent seat on the Council — a sign it was a great power again.
Kellogg–Briand Pact (1928): Germany was one of over 60 countries that agreed not to use war to settle disputes.

blocks.p: These successes restored pride and showed that co-operation could win changes. Nationalists, however, attacked Stresemann for accepting Versailles' borders in the west and for not demanding more.

sections.title: 3. How strong was the recovery?

blocks.p: Signs of strength: stable money, rising industrial output, new building, fewer political murders, and extremist parties did badly — the Nazis won only 12 seats in 1928.

Signs of weakness: the recovery depended on American loans that could be recalled at short notice; unemployment never fell much below about 1.3 million; farmers suffered from falling prices; and the middle classes who had lost their savings in 1923 did not get them back. Coalition governments still changed often.

topics.title: The rise of Hitler and the Nazis to January 1933

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Depth study 3, key topic 3. Read more: Payne, Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Germany, chapter 3 (pp. 39–59).

learn.intro: How did a small Munich party become the largest in Germany, and how did Hitler become Chancellor in January 1933 without ever winning a majority?

sections.title: 1. Hitler and the early party, 1919–22

blocks.p: Hitler joined the German Workers' Party (DAP), led by Anton Drexler, in September 1919. He was a powerful speaker and soon became its leading figure. In 1920 the party published its 25-Point Programme and renamed itself the National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP), or Nazi Party.

Changes 1920–22: Hitler became party leader in 1921; the party adopted the swastika symbol and bought a newspaper, the Völkischer Beobachter; and the SA (stormtroopers or 'Brownshirts') was set up in 1921, led by Ernst Röhm, to protect Nazi meetings and disrupt opponents'.

evidence: 1921: Hitler becomes leader; SA set up.

blocks.p: Causes: Germans were angry about the Ruhr occupation and hyperinflation; Hitler wanted to copy Mussolini's March on Rome; and the Bavarian government was right-wing, so he hoped its leaders would join him.

Events: on 8 November 1923 Hitler and the SA burst into a meeting at a Munich beer hall and forced the Bavarian leaders Kahr, Lossow and Seisser to support him. They later changed their minds. On 9 November Hitler, with the war hero General Ludendorff, marched into Munich; police opened fire and 16 Nazis were killed.

Results: the Nazi Party was banned and Hitler was put on trial. The trial gave him national publicity; the judge sentenced him to five years but he served only nine months in Landsberg prison, where he wrote Mein Kampf. He decided to win power legally, through elections.

Reorganisation 1924–28: Hitler refounded the party in 1925 and set up branches across Germany run by Gauleiters; the SS was formed as his bodyguard; the Hitler Youth was set up; Joseph Goebbels ran propaganda. But in the stable 'Golden Years' the Nazis won only 12 seats in 1928.

The Great Depression: after the Wall Street Crash (October 1929), American banks recalled their loans. German businesses closed and unemployment rose to 6 million by 1932. Coalition governments could not agree what to do, so Chancellor Brüning ruled by decree using Article 48 and cut spending, which made people suffer more.

Many Germans turned to extreme parties. The Nazis rose from 12 seats (1928) to 107 (1930) and 230 (July 1932), becoming the largest party. The Communists grew too, which frightened the middle classes and business owners.

sections.title: 4. Nazi methods and the role of the SA

ul: Propaganda: Goebbels used posters, newspapers, radio, rallies and films with simple slogans such as 'Work and Bread'.
Hitler's image: a strong leader who would make Germany great again; in 1932 he flew around Germany to speak at rallies.
Promises to everyone: jobs for workers, protection for farmers and small businesses, action against communists for the middle classes and industrialists.
Scapegoats: blaming Jews, communists and the 'November criminals' for Germany's problems.

The SA: hundreds of thousands of Brownshirts marched, protected Nazi meetings and attacked opponents, especially communists, giving an image of order and strength — while causing violence on the streets.

evidence: 1932: Hitler's flights to rallies across Germany.

sections.title: 5. From 1932 to January 1933

blocks.p: In the presidential election of 1932 Hitler won about 13 million votes but lost to Hindenburg. Brüning was replaced by Franz von Papen in May 1932. After the July 1932 election the Nazis were the largest party, but Hindenburg refused to make Hitler Chancellor.

In the November 1932 election the Nazis lost seats (196) and money was running short. Hindenburg appointed General Kurt von Schleicher as Chancellor in December, but he could not win support in the Reichstag.

Papen persuaded Hindenburg to appoint Hitler as Chancellor with Papen as Vice-Chancellor, believing that with only three Nazis in the cabinet they could control him. Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933.

evidence: 1932: Hitler wins about 13 million votes in the presidential election.

learn.intro: How did Hitler turn his position as Chancellor into a dictatorship, how did the Nazis control Germany, and how did their policies affect young people, women, the Churches, Jews and workers?

sections.title: 1. Setting up the dictatorship

blocks.p: The Reichstag Fire (27 February 1933): a Dutch communist, Marinus van der Lubbe, was arrested. Hitler claimed a communist plot; Hindenburg signed an emergency decree suspending civil rights, and thousands of communists were arrested before the March election.

The Enabling Act (23 March 1933) gave Hitler the power to make laws without the Reichstag for four years. Communist deputies were banned and the SA intimidated others. Trade unions were banned in May 1933 and by July 1933 the Nazis were the only legal party.

The Night of the Long Knives (30 June 1934): Hitler had Ernst Röhm and other SA leaders, plus political rivals, killed by the SS. The SA, which had over 2 million members, had threatened the army and wanted a 'second revolution'. The army was reassured.
When Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934, Hitler combined the posts of Chancellor and President as Führer. The army swore an oath of personal loyalty to him.

evidence: 30 June 1934: Night of the Long Knives.

blocks.p: The police state: the SS, led by Heinrich Himmler, and the Gestapo (secret police) arrested opponents; informers reported on neighbours; concentration camps such as Dachau (1933) held political prisoners; judges had to follow Nazi ideas.

Propaganda and censorship: Joseph Goebbels controlled newspapers, radio, films, books and art. Cheap radios spread Hitler's speeches; huge rallies at Nuremberg showed Nazi power; books by Jewish or 'un-German' writers were burned in 1933; the 1936 Berlin Olympics showed off Germany.

How successful? There was little open opposition, but some continued: Pastor Martin Niemöller and the Confessing Church, some young people who rejected the Hitler Youth, and underground communist and socialist groups. Many Germans conformed through fear, while others supported the regime because it brought jobs and order.

sections.title: 3. Young people, education, women and the Churches

blocks.p: Young people: boys joined the Hitler Youth and girls the League of German Maidens, with camping, sport, marching and Nazi ideas. By 1939 8 million young people were members, and membership became compulsory in 1939. In schools, teachers had to join the Nazi Teachers' League; subjects such as history and biology taught Nazi ideas about race.

Women: the Nazis wanted women to focus on 'children, kitchen, church'. Marriage loans encouraged women to leave work and have children; the Mother's Cross rewarded large families; women were removed from jobs such as doctors, lawyers and civil servants.

The Churches: Hitler signed a Concordat with the Pope in 1933, promising not to interfere with the Catholic Church, but later broke it. The Nazis set up a Reich Church for Protestants; Pastor Niemöller's Confessing Church opposed it, and Niemöller was sent to a concentration camp.

evidence: 8 million young people in Nazi youth groups by 1939.

sections.title: 4. Racial policy and the persecution of Jews

blocks.p: The Nazis believed in an 'Aryan' master race and treated Jews as enemies. Persecution increased step by step:

ul: April 1933: a boycott of Jewish shops; Jews dismissed from the civil service.
September 1935: the Nuremberg Laws took away Jews' German citizenship and banned marriages between Jews and non-Jews.

9–10 November 1938: Kristallnacht ('Night of Broken Glass') — synagogues, shops and homes attacked; around 100 Jews killed and about 30,000 Jewish men sent to concentration camps. Jews were then fined 1 billion marks.

blocks.p: When Hitler came to power 6 million Germans were unemployed; by 1939 this was reduced to about half a million. Methods: the National Labour Service (RAD) gave young men work on projects such as autobahns; rearmament created jobs in factories; conscription (from 1935) took nearly 1 million men into the armed forces; and women and Jews dismissed from jobs were not counted ('invisible unemployment').

Trade unions were replaced by the German Labour Front (DAF), which controlled wages and hours. Strength Through Joy (KdF) offered cheap holidays, concerts and sport, and a scheme to save for a Volkswagen 'people's car'. Workers had jobs, but longer hours and no right to strike.

learn.intro: During the war the Nazis murdered millions of Jews in the Holocaust. At home, Germans faced rationing, 'total war' and Allied bombing, and some began to resist. The Third Reich ended with Hitler's death in 1945.

blocks.p: Conquest brought millions more Jews under Nazi control — there were 3 million Jews in Poland alone. Jews were forced into ghettos, walled-off areas of cities such as Warsaw and Łódź, where many died from hunger and disease.
After the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941, SS death squads (Einsatzgruppen) followed the army and shot Jews and others in mass killings.

At the Wannsee Conference in January 1942, Nazi leaders organised the 'Final Solution' — the plan to murder all of Europe's Jews. Jews were transported to death camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau and Treblinka and killed in gas chambers. Almost 6 million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust, along with millions of others, including Roma, disabled people and Soviet prisoners.

sections.title: 2. The Home Front

blocks.p: Rationing of food and clothing began in 1939. At first Germans were protected by food taken from occupied countries, but rations were cut as the war went badly, and shortages grew worse from 1942.

Total war: after defeat at Stalingrad, Goebbels announced 'total war' in February 1943 — every part of the economy and society was to work for the war. Places of entertainment closed and more people were directed into war work.

The changing role of women: Nazi ideas said women belonged at home, so at first the regime avoided conscripting them. As the labour shortage grew, more women were drawn into work — by mid-1943 half a million extra women were working in industry — though Germany relied heavily on foreign forced labourers and prisoners: about 7 million were working for German industry.

Allied bombing: British and American bombing destroyed cities. Raids on Hamburg in July 1943 killed 42,600 civilians and forced around 1 million others to flee; Dresden was devastated in February 1945. Bombing damaged homes, factories and morale, and millions of children were evacuated to the countryside.

evidence: About 7 million foreign workers and prisoners in German industry.

ul: Edelweiss Pirates: groups of working-class young people who rejected the Hitler Youth, sang banned songs and attacked Hitler Youth patrols; some helped deserters. In 1944 thirteen members were publicly hanged in Cologne.
The White Rose: students at Munich University, including Hans and Sophie Scholl, who distributed leaflets calling for resistance. They were caught in February 1943 and executed.

The July Bomb Plot (20 July 1944): army officers led by Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg planted a bomb at Hitler's headquarters. Hitler survived; the plotters were executed and thousands of suspects arrested.

blocks.p: Opposition grew as Germany began to lose the war, but it never became a mass movement because of terror and the risk of execution.

sections.title: 4. The end of the Third Reich

blocks.p: By 1945 Soviet forces were advancing from the east and British and American forces from the west. Hitler stayed in his bunker in Berlin and killed himself on 30 April 1945 as Soviet troops reached the city. Germany surrendered on 7–8 May 1945.
Millions of Germans fled or were expelled from the east, and Germany was occupied and divided by the Allies.

learn.intro: After 1945 Americans feared communism abroad and spies at home. Senator Joseph McCarthy exploited that fear — until television helped bring him down.

blocks.p: The Cold War, 1945–50: the USSR took control of Eastern Europe; the Berlin Blockade (1948–49) raised tension; in 1949 the USSR tested an atomic bomb and China became communist; in June 1950 the Korean War began. Many Americans felt communism was spreading and feared enemies inside the USA.

Spy cases seemed to prove the danger. Alger Hiss, a former State Department official, was accused in 1948 of spying for the USSR and convicted of perjury (lying under oath) in 1950. Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were arrested in 1950 for passing atomic secrets and executed in 1953.

Government action: President Truman's Loyalty Program (1947) investigated millions of federal employees. The FBI under J. Edgar Hoover watched suspected communists. The House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) investigated Hollywood: in 1947 the 'Hollywood Ten' refused to answer its questions, were jailed and blacklisted.

sections.title: 2. McCarthy's methods and the growth of opposition

blocks.p: On 9 February 1950, in a speech at Wheeling, West Virginia, Senator Joseph McCarthy claimed to have a list of 205 communists working in the State Department. He never produced proof.

His methods: making accusations without evidence, changing his numbers, smearing opponents as 'soft on communism', bullying witnesses at hearings, and using the press to spread his claims. From 1953 he chaired a Senate investigations subcommittee. People feared that if they criticised him they would be accused next.

Opposition grew. In June 1950 Senator Margaret Chase Smith made her 'Declaration of Conscience' speech against his tactics. In March 1954 journalist Edward R. Murrow's television programme See It Now exposed McCarthy's methods.

evidence: June 1950: Margaret Chase Smith's 'Declaration of Conscience'.

sections.title: 3. McCarthy's downfall and the impact of McCarthyism

blocks.p: McCarthy went too far when he accused the US Army of hiding communists. The Army–McCarthy hearings (April–June 1954) were shown on television to millions. Viewers saw him bully witnesses; the Army's lawyer Joseph Welch asked, 'Have you no sense of decency, sir?' His popularity collapsed. In December 1954 the Senate voted to censure him. He died in 1957.

Impact: thousands lost their jobs; blacklists damaged careers in film, education and government; loyalty oaths spread; people were afraid to express opinions or join organisations, and free speech suffered. It also made anti-communism a central part of US politics for decades.

learn.intro: In 1950 black Americans in the South lived under segregation and most could not vote. In the 1950s the Supreme Court, ordinary people and courageous campaigns began to challenge this.

sections.title: 1. Segregation, discrimination, the courts and Congress

blocks.p: In the southern states 'Jim Crow' laws segregated schools, transport, restaurants and even water fountains. Most black southerners could not vote because of literacy tests, poll taxes and intimidation. In the North there was no legal segregation, but discrimination in housing and jobs kept many black Americans in poor areas (ghettos).

The Supreme Court could overturn unfair laws, and the NAACP used court cases to challenge segregation. Congress was slow to act, because southern Democrats held powerful positions and used the filibuster to block civil rights bills.

evidence: Southern segregation in schools, transport and public places.
Literacy tests and poll taxes kept black southerners from voting.

sections.title: 2. Brown v Board of Education and Emmett Till

blocks.p: In 1954 the NAACP's lawyer Thurgood Marshall won Brown v Board of Education of Topeka. The Supreme Court, led by Chief Justice Earl Warren, ruled unanimously that segregated schools were unconstitutional. But in 1955 it only said desegregation should happen 'with all deliberate speed', so many southern states delayed.

In August 1955 Emmett Till, a 14-year-old black boy from Chicago, was murdered in Mississippi for supposedly whistling at a white woman. His mother insisted on an open-casket funeral, and photographs shocked the nation. His killers were found not guilty by an all-white jury and later admitted the murder. The case pushed many to act.

evidence: August 1955: Emmett Till murdered; killers acquitted.

sections.title: 3. Montgomery and Little Rock

blocks.p: On 1 December 1955 Rosa Parks, an NAACP secretary, was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white man. Black residents boycotted the buses for 381 days, organised by the Montgomery Improvement Association led by Martin Luther King. In 1956 the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional. The boycott showed the power of peaceful mass protest and made King a national leader.

In September 1957 nine black students tried to attend Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas. Governor Orval Faubus used the National Guard to keep them out and white mobs abused them. President Eisenhower sent federal troops to protect the 'Little Rock Nine' — showing the federal government would enforce the law, although it acted reluctantly.

evidence: September 1957: Little Rock; Eisenhower sends troops.

sections.title: 4. The Civil Rights Act 1957 and the revival of the KKK

blocks.p: The Civil Rights Act of 1957 was the first civil rights law since Reconstruction. It set up a Civil Rights Commission and a Civil Rights Division in the Justice Department to deal with voting rights. It was weakened by southern senators and did little in practice, but it was a significant start.
White resistance grew: White Citizens' Councils organised against desegregation, and the Ku Klux Klan revived, using intimidation, bombings and murder.

evidence: 1957: Civil Rights Act — Commission and Justice Department division.

topics.title: The impact of civil rights protests, 1960–74

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Depth study 7, key topic 3.

learn.intro: In the 1960s sit-ins, Freedom Rides and mass marches forced the federal government to pass major civil rights laws. Later in the decade, frustration led many towards Black Power.

sections.title: 1. Sit-ins, Freedom Riders and the Meredith case

blocks.p: Sit-ins: on 1 February 1960 four black students sat at a whites-only lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and refused to leave. Sit-ins spread across the South, and many lunch counters desegregated. The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) was set up in April 1960.

Freedom Rides (1961): CORE sent black and white volunteers on buses through the South to test whether bus stations obeyed the law against segregation. At Anniston, Alabama, a bus was firebombed (May 1961); in Birmingham riders were beaten. The government eventually enforced desegregation of bus terminals.

Voting rights and the Meredith case: in 1962 James Meredith tried to enrol at the University of Mississippi. Riots broke out and two people were killed; President Kennedy sent federal marshals and troops, and Meredith graduated in 1963.

evidence: 1962: James Meredith at the University of Mississippi.

sections.title: 2. Martin Luther King's methods and campaigns

blocks.p: King believed in non-violent direct action: peaceful protest that would provoke a violent response from racists, which the media would show to the world, forcing the government to act.

Birmingham, Alabama (1963): police chief 'Bull' Connor used dogs and fire hoses on protesters, including children. Television pictures shocked the nation and President Kennedy proposed a civil rights bill.
The March on Washington (28 August 1963): about 250,000 people marched; King gave his 'I have a dream' speech, showing the movement's huge support.

Mississippi Freedom Summer (1964): volunteers registered black voters; three workers — James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner — were murdered. The Civil Rights Act (July 1964) banned segregation in public places and discrimination in jobs.
Selma (1965): marchers for voting rights were attacked by police on 'Bloody Sunday' (7 March). Shocked by the pictures, Congress passed the Voting Rights Act (August 1965), banning literacy tests.

sections.title: 3. The Nation of Islam, Malcolm X and Black Power

blocks.p: The Nation of Islam called for black separation, not integration. Its best-known speaker, Malcolm X, criticised King's non-violence and argued black people should defend themselves 'by any means necessary'. He left the Nation of Islam in 1964 and was assassinated in February 1965.

Reasons for Black Power: slow progress in the North, poverty in the ghettos, police brutality, and anger at the violence used against peaceful protesters. In 1966 Stokely Carmichael of SNCC popularised the slogan 'Black Power', meaning black pride and black control of black communities.

Race riots: in August 1965 riots in the Watts district of Los Angeles left 34 dead; more riots followed in other cities. The Black Panthers, founded in 1966 by Bobby Seale and Huey Newton, carried guns to monitor the police and ran community programmes such as free breakfasts for children.
1968 Olympics: in Mexico City, US athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised black-gloved fists on the medal podium — a Black Power salute seen around the world.

topics.title: Other protest movements: students, women, anti-Vietnam

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Depth study 7, key topic 4.

learn.intro: Inspired by the civil rights movement and angered by the Vietnam War, students and women organised their own protests in the 1960s and early 1970s — and provoked opposition.

sections.title: 1. Why protest movements grew

ul: The baby boom: millions of young people, many at rapidly expanding universities.
The civil rights movement showed that protest could work and taught methods such as sit-ins and marches.
The Vietnam War: young men could be drafted (conscripted); television showed the war's horrors.
A new youth culture questioned traditional values.

evidence: Rapid growth of universities in the 1960s.

sections.title: 2. The student movement and anti-Vietnam War protest

blocks.p: Students for a Democratic Society (SDS), founded in 1960, called for 'participatory democracy' and became a leading anti-war group. In 1964 the Berkeley Free Speech Movement at the University of California protested against a ban on political activity on campus, using sit-ins.

As the war escalated from 1965, students held teach-ins, burned draft cards and organised huge marches. At Kent State University in May 1970, National Guard troops shot dead four students during an anti-war protest, shocking the nation.
'Hippies' rejected mainstream society, promoting peace, love and alternative lifestyles; the Woodstock festival (1969) became a symbol of the counter-culture.

evidence: May 1970: Kent State — four students killed.

sections.title: 3. The women's movement

blocks.p: Eleanor Roosevelt chaired President Kennedy's Commission on the Status of Women (1961), whose 1963 report showed widespread discrimination. The Equal Pay Act (1963) required equal pay for equal work.

Betty Friedan's book The Feminine Mystique (1963) described the frustration of many middle-class housewives. In 1966 she helped found the National Organization for Women (NOW), which campaigned for equal rights through the law and politics.

The more radical women's liberation movement challenged traditional roles and beauty standards — for example the protest at the Miss America contest in 1968. In Roe v Wade (1973) the Supreme Court ruled that women had a right to abortion.

evidence: 1963: The Feminine Mystique; Equal Pay Act.

sections.title: 4. Opposition to the women's movement

blocks.p: Many Americans, including many women, opposed feminism. Phyllis Schlafly led the STOP ERA campaign (from 1972) against the Equal Rights Amendment, which Congress passed in 1972. She argued it would harm traditional families and remove protections for women, such as exemption from the draft. The ERA was never ratified by enough states.
Religious and conservative groups also opposed abortion after Roe v Wade, and the 'pro-life' movement grew.

evidence: 1972: ERA passed by Congress; STOP ERA begins.

learn.intro: A break-in at the Democratic Party's offices in 1972 grew into a scandal that forced President Nixon to resign in 1974 — the only US President ever to do so — and led to new laws limiting presidential power.

sections.title: 1. Reasons for and key features of the scandal

blocks.p: Nixon was secretive and suspicious of opponents; he kept an 'enemies list' and his Committee for the Re-election of the President (nicknamed CREEP) used dirty tricks. On 17 June 1972 five men were arrested breaking into the Democratic National Committee's offices in the Watergate building in Washington, DC. They were linked to CREEP.

Nixon won a landslide re-election in November 1972, but Washington Post journalists Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein, helped by a secret source ('Deep Throat'), kept investigating. A Senate committee held televised hearings in 1973. White House counsel John Dean testified that Nixon was involved in a cover-up, and an aide revealed that Nixon secretly taped conversations in his office.

Nixon refused to hand over the tapes. In October 1973 he had the special prosecutor, Archibald Cox, sacked (the 'Saturday Night Massacre'). In July 1974 the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in US v Nixon that he must release them, and the House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment. One tape — the 'smoking gun' — showed he had ordered the cover-up. Nixon resigned on 9 August 1974.

sections.title: 2. Impact on Nixon, US politics and new laws

blocks.p: Nixon became the first President to resign. Gerald Ford became President. On 8 September 1974 Ford gave Nixon a full pardon for any crimes — many Americans were angry, and it probably helped Ford lose the 1976 election.
Trust in government fell sharply. Democrats made big gains in the 1974 congressional elections. The media's investigative role grew.

Election Campaign Act (1974): limits on campaign donations and spending; a Federal Election Commission.
Privacy Act (1974): limited how the government could collect and use information about individuals.
Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act (1974): stopped the President refusing to spend money Congress had approved.

topics.title: Progress in the mid-19th century: Nightingale, Chadwick, Snow and Simpson

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Breadth study B2, key topic 1. No class textbook uploaded for this option yet.

learn.intro: In the mid-1800s nobody knew that germs caused disease. Even so, Nightingale improved hospitals, Simpson tackled pain in surgery, Chadwick pushed for public health reform and Snow linked cholera to dirty water.

sections.title: 1. Barriers to progress

blocks.p: The biggest barrier was the lack of understanding of what caused disease. Most doctors believed in miasma — that disease spread through bad air from rotting matter. Some believed in spontaneous generation, the idea that microbes appeared from decaying material. Without knowing about germs, doctors could not prevent infection.

Other barriers: cities were overcrowded with poor housing, little clean water and no proper sewers; governments believed in laissez-faire (not interfering in people's lives); and many doctors resisted new ideas.

evidence: Industrial towns overcrowded with poor sanitation.

sections.title: 2. Florence Nightingale and nursing

blocks.p: During the Crimean War, Florence Nightingale took 38 nurses to the army hospital at Scutari in 1854. She found filthy wards, poor food and overcrowding. She cleaned the hospital, improved hygiene, food and ventilation, and organised the nurses. The death rate among soldiers in the hospital fell dramatically.

Back in Britain she used statistics to argue for reform, wrote Notes on Nursing (1859), and in 1860 opened the Nightingale School of Nursing at St Thomas' Hospital, London. Nursing became a respectable, trained profession for women. She also influenced hospital design, favouring airy 'pavilion' wards — although she believed in miasma rather than germs.

evidence: 1854: Nightingale arrives at Scutari with 38 nurses.

sections.title: 3. Dangers in surgery and Simpson's chloroform

blocks.p: Surgery had three great dangers: pain, infection and bleeding. Without pain relief, surgeons had to operate very quickly; patients could die of shock.

In 1847 James Simpson, an Edinburgh professor, discovered that chloroform was an effective anaesthetic. It became popular after Queen Victoria used it during childbirth in 1853. There was opposition: some patients died from overdoses (Hannah Greener died in 1848), and some people believed pain was natural or God-given.

Anaesthetics solved pain, but surgeons now attempted longer, more complicated operations — so deaths from infection and bleeding could actually rise. This period is sometimes called the 'black period' of surgery.

sections.title: 4. Public health: Chadwick, the 1848 Act, cholera and Snow

blocks.p: Edwin Chadwick's Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population (1842) showed that the poor in towns died much younger than the rich, and argued that cleaning up towns would save money by reducing illness.

Cholera epidemics (1831–32, 1848–49, 1853–54) killed tens of thousands and frightened the government. The Public Health Act (1848) set up a General Board of Health and allowed towns to create local boards of health to improve water and sewers — but it was permissive (not compulsory), so many towns did nothing.

In 1854 John Snow mapped cholera deaths in Soho, London, and showed they clustered around the Broad Street water pump. He had the pump handle removed and cases fell. He proved cholera spread through contaminated water, not miasma — though he could not identify the germ, and many ignored his findings at first.

evidence: 1854: Snow and the Broad Street pump.

topics.title: Discovery and development, 1860–75: Lister and Pasteur

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Breadth study B2, key topic 2.

learn.intro: Pasteur's germ theory transformed understanding of disease. Lister used it to fight infection in surgery, Parliament passed a compulsory Public Health Act, and Elizabeth Garrett broke into the male world of medicine.

blocks.p: Louis Pasteur, a French chemist, was asked to find out why wine and beer went sour. He showed that microbes (germs) in the air caused decay. In 1861, using swan-necked flasks, he showed that liquid stayed fresh when microbes from the air could not reach it — disproving spontaneous generation.

Effects: germ theory showed that microbes cause decay and, as later work proved, disease. It gave a scientific reason for cleanliness, led to antiseptics in surgery, and made identifying specific germs and developing vaccines possible. Many doctors were slow to accept it.

sections.title: 2. Lister and antiseptics

blocks.p: Joseph Lister, a surgeon in Glasgow, read Pasteur's work and thought germs might cause infection in wounds. In 1865 he used carbolic acid on the wound of an 11-year-old boy, James Greenlees, who had a compound fracture; the wound healed without infection.

Lister soaked dressings and instruments in carbolic acid and sprayed it in the air during operations. He published his results in 1867: death rates in his operations fell sharply. There was opposition: carbolic acid irritated skin, the methods slowed operations, and many surgeons did not accept germ theory.

evidence: 1865: Lister treats James Greenlees with carbolic acid.

sections.title: 3. The Public Health Act 1875

blocks.p: By the 1870s attitudes were changing: working men in towns had the vote from 1867, so politicians needed their support; germ theory and Snow's work showed the link between dirt and disease; and Bazalgette's new London sewers (built after the 'Great Stink' of 1858) showed what could be done.

The Public Health Act of 1875 was compulsory. Councils had to provide clean water, remove sewage, and appoint a Medical Officer of Health and sanitary inspectors. It marked the end of laissez-faire in public health.

evidence: 1867: more working men get the vote.

sections.title: 4. Hospitals, nursing and women in medicine

blocks.p: Nightingale's influence continued: trained nurses spread, and new hospitals used her pavilion design with light, airy, easily cleaned wards.

Elizabeth Garrett was refused entry to medical schools because she was a woman. She found a loophole: the Society of Apothecaries had not banned women, and in 1865 she gained its licence, becoming the first woman to qualify in Britain. She opened a dispensary for women in London and later gained a medical degree in Paris (1870). The Medical Act of 1876 allowed women to qualify as doctors.

evidence: 1865: Garrett qualifies through the Society of Apothecaries.

topics.title: Accelerating change, 1875–1905: Ehrlich, Koch and chemistry

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Breadth study B2, key topic 3.

learn.intro: Scientists began to identify the germs behind specific diseases. Surgery moved from killing germs to keeping them out altogether, public health improved under the 1875 Act, and chemistry and physics opened new possibilities.

sections.title: 1. Koch and bacteriology

blocks.p: Robert Koch, a German doctor, proved that specific germs cause specific diseases. He identified the anthrax bacterium (1876), the tuberculosis bacterium (1882) and the cholera bacterium (1883). He developed methods to grow bacteria on solid agar and to stain them with dyes so they could be seen under a microscope.

Rivalry between France (Pasteur) and Germany (Koch) speeded up research. Pasteur developed vaccines for chicken cholera (1879), anthrax (1881) and rabies (1885), building on Edward Jenner's earlier smallpox vaccine.

evidence: 1876: anthrax; 1882: tuberculosis; 1883: cholera — all identified by Koch.

blocks.p: Antiseptic surgery killed germs with chemicals. From the 1880s surgeons moved to aseptic surgery — preventing germs from entering the wound at all. Instruments were sterilised with steam, operating theatres were cleaned thoroughly, and surgeons wore gowns, masks and caps. Rubber gloves were introduced in 1890 (by the American surgeon William Halsted).
With pain controlled by anaesthetics and infection reduced by aseptic methods, surgeons could attempt longer and more complex operations inside the body. Bleeding remained the main problem.

sections.title: 3. The impact of the Public Health Act 1875

blocks.p: Because the 1875 Act was compulsory, towns built sewers and reservoirs, provided clean water, and appointed Medical Officers of Health. Cholera epidemics ended in Britain after 1866. Death rates in towns fell, though poor housing and poverty still caused high infant mortality.

evidence: No major cholera epidemic in Britain after 1866.
Councils provided sewers and clean water under the 1875 Act.

sections.title: 4. Science and medicine: blood, magic bullets and radiation

blocks.p: Blood transfusions: early transfusions often failed because the patient's body rejected the blood. In 1901 Karl Landsteiner discovered blood groups, explaining why — though blood could not yet be stored because it clotted.

Magic bullets: Paul Ehrlich, who had worked with Koch, searched for chemicals that would kill a specific germ without harming the patient. After hundreds of tests, his team found Salvarsan 606 (1909), the first 'magic bullet', which cured syphilis.

Radioactivity: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895, allowing doctors to see bones and objects inside the body. Marie Curie and Pierre Curie discovered radium and polonium in 1898; radium was used to treat cancer. Marie Curie later developed mobile X-ray units in the First World War.

learn.intro: The Liberal governments of 1906–11 took new responsibility for people's health. Then the First World War created terrible wounds — and pushed forward surgery, X-rays, blood transfusion and the role of women in medicine.

blocks.p: Why? Surveys by Charles Booth (London) and Seebohm Rowntree (York) showed that about a third of people lived in poverty. During the Boer War (1899–1902) many volunteers were rejected as unfit, worrying the government about national strength. The new Labour Party competed for working-class votes, and Liberal politicians such as David Lloyd George and Winston Churchill wanted reform.

ul: 1906: free school meals for poor children.
1907: school medical inspections — the School Medical Service.
1908: old-age pensions for over-70s.
1911: National Insurance Act — workers paid in to receive sick pay and free treatment from a doctor (but not their families).

blocks.p: Impact: the government accepted responsibility for health and welfare, children's health improved, and some sick workers were protected. But wives, children and the unemployed were often left out, and hospital treatment was not covered.

sections.title: 2. The First World War: surgery and treatment

blocks.p: Trench warfare caused huge numbers of wounds from shells and bullets, often infected by soil bacteria (gas gangrene). Doctors developed debridement (cutting away dead tissue), and Carrel–Dakin solution to irrigate wounds.
The Thomas splint kept broken legs still and greatly reduced deaths from fractures of the thigh bone. Harold Gillies pioneered plastic surgery to rebuild faces at Queen's Hospital, Sidcup (1917).
X-rays: mobile X-ray units — including those organised by Marie Curie — found bullets and shrapnel near the front line.
Blood transfusion: adding sodium citrate stopped blood clotting, so blood could be stored. In 1917 a blood depot was set up before the Battle of Cambrai.

evidence: Thomas splint reduced deaths from thigh fractures.
1917: Gillies at Sidcup; blood stored before Cambrai.

sections.title: 3. The war and women in medicine

blocks.p: Thousands of women served as nurses, including volunteers in the Voluntary Aid Detachments (VADs) and the First Aid Nursing Yeomanry (FANY), who drove ambulances. Women doctors such as Elsie Inglis set up the Scottish Women's Hospitals, which worked in France and Serbia, after the War Office initially refused her help.
The war showed women's skill and courage, and more medical schools admitted women — though many restrictions returned after 1918.

evidence: Elsie Inglis and the Scottish Women's Hospitals.

timeline.event: Gillies opens Queen's Hospital, Sidcup; blood stored before Cambrai
