topics.title: Advances in medicine, surgery and public health, 1920–48: the NHS

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Breadth study B2, key topic 5.

learn.intro: Penicillin became the first mass-produced antibiotic, the Second World War pushed surgery forward again, and the Beveridge Report led to the creation of the NHS in 1948.

sections.title: 1. Penicillin: Fleming, Florey and Chain

blocks.p: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that mould (penicillium) had killed bacteria on a culture plate at St Mary's Hospital, London. He published his findings but lacked the funding and chemists to produce enough penicillin to use as a medicine.

From 1938 Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford worked out how to purify penicillin and tested it on mice (1940) and then on a patient, the policeman Albert Alexander (1941), who improved before supplies ran out.

British firms were busy with war production, so Florey went to the USA. After the USA entered the war, the government funded mass production; by D-Day (June 1944) there was enough penicillin to treat Allied casualties. After the war it became widely available and led to other antibiotics.

evidence: 1940–41: Florey and Chain's tests; Albert Alexander.

sections.title: 2. The Second World War: surgery, blood and women

blocks.p: Skin grafts: Archibald McIndoe treated badly burned RAF pilots at East Grinstead, developing new skin-graft techniques. His patients formed the 'Guinea Pig Club' and he helped them return to normal life.
Blood transfusion: blood banks stored large amounts of blood for air-raid victims and soldiers; the National Blood Transfusion Service followed in 1946.
Women in medicine: more women trained and worked as doctors and nurses during the war, and the Goodenough Report (1944) recommended that all medical schools should admit women.

evidence: McIndoe at East Grinstead; the Guinea Pig Club.

sections.title: 3. Beveridge and the NHS

blocks.p: The Beveridge Report (1942) identified 'five giants' to defeat — Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness — and proposed a welfare state with a national health service. The war had shown what government organisation could do (the Emergency Medical Service), and people wanted a fairer society.

The Labour government elected in 1945 introduced the NHS. Aneurin Bevan, the Health Minister, overcame opposition from many doctors by allowing them to keep private patients. The NHS began on 5 July 1948, free at the point of use for everyone.

Importance for public health: everyone could see a doctor, get hospital treatment, glasses and dentures without paying; demand was huge; vaccination and health visiting were organised nationally. Access to health care was transformed — though costs rose quickly.

questions.label: Adapted from the Arcadia IGCSE model paragraphs
questions.q:
How far was the discovery of penicillin in the 1920s a key turning point in the treatment of disease?
Explain your answer.

model.t: The discovery of penicillin was a turning point to a large extent because it transformed the treatment of infection.
Firstly, Alexander Fleming identified penicillin in 1928 as the first effective antibiotic. This shows that treatment could now kill bacteria, rather than just manage symptoms.
Secondly, in the 1940s Florey and Chain developed methods to mass-produce penicillin, which saved thousands of lives during the Second World War.

Finally, after the war penicillin became widely available and inspired other antibiotics such as streptomycin. This was significant because it marked a permanent change in the treatment of disease, making bacterial infections curable rather than fatal.

topics.title: The struggle against France for independence, 1945–54

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Historical investigation A4, key topic 1. No class textbook uploaded for this option yet.

learn.intro: After the Second World War, Ho Chi Minh's Vietminh declared Vietnamese independence. France tried to take back its colony, leading to eight years of war that ended in French defeat at Dien Bien Phu.

sections.title: 1. Origins of the First Indochina War and the aims of the Vietminh

blocks.p: Vietnam had been part of French Indochina since the late 1800s. During the Second World War Japan occupied it. In 1941 Ho Chi Minh, a communist and nationalist, set up the Vietminh (League for the Independence of Vietnam) to fight the Japanese and the French.

When Japan surrendered, Ho declared Vietnamese independence in Hanoi on 2 September 1945, quoting the American Declaration of Independence. But France wanted its colony back. Talks failed, and after French ships shelled Haiphong in November 1946, full war began in December 1946.
The Vietminh's aims: full independence from France, a united Vietnam, land for peasants, and a communist government. Their message of independence and land reform won wide peasant support.

sections.title: 2. General Giap's tactics and the search for a solution

blocks.p: General Vo Nguyen Giap commanded the Vietminh army. Following Mao's ideas, he used guerrilla warfare: small units, ambushes, hit-and-run attacks and support from villagers, avoiding large battles while the French were stronger. The aim was to wear the French down and only fight conventional battles once strong enough.

After the communists won in China in 1949, the Vietminh received Chinese weapons, training and safe bases. The USA, fearing the spread of communism, paid an increasing share of France's war costs — by 1954 most of them.
France looked for a way out. Peace talks began at the Geneva Conference in April 1954, while the decisive battle was being fought.

evidence: 1949: communist victory in China brings aid to the Vietminh.
By 1954 the USA paid most of France's war costs.

sections.title: 3. Dien Bien Phu and its consequences

blocks.p: In November 1953 the French built a fortified base at Dien Bien Phu, in a valley near the Laos border, hoping to lure the Vietminh into a battle they would lose. Instead, Giap's forces dragged heavy artillery up the surrounding hills by hand and surrounded the base.

The siege began on 13 March 1954. Vietminh artillery destroyed the airstrip, so the French could only be supplied by parachute. The base surrendered on 7 May 1954, and thousands of French troops were captured.

Immediate consequences: France decided to leave Indochina. The Geneva Agreements (July 1954) recognised the independence of Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia and temporarily divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel — communist North under Ho, non-communist South — with national elections promised for 1956.

evidence: November 1953: French base at Dien Bien Phu.
July 1954: Geneva Agreements — division at the 17th parallel; elections promised for 1956.

learn.intro: After Geneva, the USA backed a non-communist South Vietnam to stop the 'dominoes' falling. But Diem's government was unpopular, the NLF grew, and by 1964 the USA was on the edge of full-scale war.

sections.title: 1. Geneva, the domino theory and the formation of South Vietnam

blocks.p: The Geneva Conference (1954) aimed to end the war and divide Vietnam temporarily, with elections in 1956. The USA did not sign the agreement; it feared Ho Chi Minh would win any election.

President Eisenhower explained US policy with the domino theory (1954): if one country fell to communism, its neighbours would follow, like a row of dominoes. The USA set up SEATO (1954) and supported a separate state in the South.
Ngo Dinh Diem became leader of South Vietnam (the Republic of Vietnam) after a rigged referendum in 1955. With US support he refused to hold the 1956 elections.

sections.title: 2. Life in North and South Vietnam

blocks.p: North (Ho Chi Minh): a communist state. Land reform (1953–56) took land from landlords and gave it to peasants, but it was carried out brutally and thousands were killed; Ho later admitted mistakes. Industry and farming were brought under state control.

South (Ngo Dinh Diem): Diem was a Catholic in a mainly Buddhist country and favoured Catholics and his own family; his brother Nhu ran the secret police. Land reform helped landlords more than peasants. Opponents were imprisoned and corruption was widespread, so the government lost support in the countryside.

evidence: 1953–56: brutal land reform in the North.
Diem favoured Catholics; his brother Nhu ran the secret police.

sections.title: 3. Ho's policies to unite Vietnam: the NLF and the Ho Chi Minh Trail

blocks.p: Ho was determined to unite Vietnam. In December 1960 the National Liberation Front (NLF) was set up in the South, with Northern backing, to overthrow Diem. Its fighters were called the Vietcong by their enemies. They used guerrilla tactics and won peasant support by redistributing land, though they also used terror against officials.
The Ho Chi Minh Trail — a network of paths through Laos and Cambodia — carried soldiers and supplies from North to South. It was very hard to cut because it ran through jungle and neutral countries.

evidence: The Ho Chi Minh Trail ran through Laos and Cambodia.

sections.title: 4. The US response, the fall of Diem and the Gulf of Tonkin

blocks.p: The USA sent money, weapons and military advisers. Under President Kennedy the number of advisers rose from under 1,000 in 1961 to about 16,000 by 1963.

The Strategic Hamlet Programme (1962) moved peasants into fortified villages to cut them off from the Vietcong. Peasants resented being moved from their land and ancestral graves; many hamlets were badly built and infiltrated, and the programme increased support for the NLF.

In 1963 Buddhist protests grew; the monk Thich Quang Duc burned himself to death in Saigon in June, and the photographs shocked the world. With US approval, South Vietnamese generals overthrew Diem in November 1963; he and Nhu were killed. Unstable military governments followed.

In August 1964 the US destroyer Maddox reported attacks by North Vietnamese boats in the Gulf of Tonkin (the second attack probably did not happen). Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, allowing President Johnson to take 'all necessary measures' — a blank cheque for war.

topics.title: Increased US involvement in the war, 1964–68

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Historical investigation A4, key topic 3.

learn.intro: After the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, President Johnson turned an advisory mission into a full-scale war. Huge US firepower could not defeat the Vietcong's guerrilla tactics, and the Tet Offensive of 1968 became the turning point.

sections.title: 1. Escalation: Rolling Thunder and US ground troops

blocks.p: In February 1965, after Vietcong attacks on US bases such as Pleiku, Johnson began Operation Rolling Thunder — a sustained bombing campaign against North Vietnam that lasted until 1968. Its aims were to destroy industry and supply routes, stop the flow of men and materials south, and force Hanoi to negotiate.
In March 1965 the first US combat troops — Marines — landed at Da Nang to protect the air base. Numbers rose rapidly: about 184,000 by the end of 1965 and over 500,000 by 1968.
Rolling Thunder did not achieve its aims. North Vietnam had little industry to destroy, supplies kept moving down the Ho Chi Minh Trail, and the bombing hardened Northern resistance.

evidence: March 1965: Marines land at Da Nang.

sections.title: 2. Vietcong tactics

blocks.p: The Vietcong avoided open battles with the much better-armed Americans. They used guerrilla tactics: ambushes, hit-and-run attacks, and booby traps such as punji sticks and tripwire mines, which caused many US casualties and destroyed morale.

They built huge tunnel networks, such as at Cu Chi near Saigon, with living quarters, hospitals and storerooms, so they could hide and appear behind American lines. They mixed with the villagers, so US soldiers could not tell friend from enemy.
'Hugging' tactics — fighting very close to US troops — meant the Americans could not call in air strikes or artillery without hitting their own men.

evidence: Booby traps such as punji sticks.

sections.title: 3. US tactics: search and destroy, Agent Orange and napalm

blocks.p: General Westmoreland's strategy was attrition: kill enemy soldiers faster than they could be replaced. Search and destroy missions sent troops, often by helicopter, to find and kill Vietcong in villages. Success was measured by 'body counts', which encouraged soldiers to count any dead Vietnamese as Vietcong and turned villagers against the USA.

Chemical weapons were used on a huge scale. Agent Orange, a defoliant, was sprayed to strip jungle cover and destroy crops; it caused long-term illness and birth defects. Napalm, a burning jelly dropped in bombs, killed and maimed civilians as well as fighters.
US troops were often young conscripts serving one-year tours, unfamiliar with the country and under constant threat. Morale fell and drug use rose.

evidence: Agent Orange stripped jungle cover and crops.
One-year tours of duty for US conscripts.

sections.title: 4. The Tet Offensive, 1968

blocks.p: On 30–31 January 1968, during the Tet (Vietnamese New Year) holiday truce, about 80,000 Vietcong and North Vietnamese troops attacked over 100 towns and cities across South Vietnam, including Saigon, where they briefly got inside the US Embassy compound. The ancient city of Hue was held for nearly a month. The offensive followed a diversionary siege of the US base at Khe Sanh, which began on 21 January 1968.
Militarily, Tet was a defeat for the communists: they suffered very heavy losses, the Vietcong was badly weakened, and the expected popular uprising in the South did not happen.

Politically, it was a turning point. Americans had been told the war was being won; TV showed fighting in the US Embassy. Respected newsreader Walter Cronkite said the war was a stalemate. Westmoreland asked for 206,000 more troops and was refused. On 31 March 1968 Johnson announced a partial halt to the bombing and said he would not stand for re-election.
In March 1968 US soldiers killed several hundred unarmed villagers at My Lai. The massacre was covered up and only became public in November 1969, further damaging support for the war.

evidence: 31 March 1968: Johnson will not stand again.
My Lai: March 1968; made public November 1969.

learn.intro: Nixon promised 'peace with honour'. He withdrew US troops through Vietnamisation while widening the war into Cambodia and Laos. The Paris Peace Accords of 1973 ended US involvement, and Saigon fell to the North in 1975.

blocks.p: Richard Nixon became President in January 1969 promising to end the war with 'peace with honour'. His policy of Vietnamisation meant handing the fighting over to the South Vietnamese army (ARVN), which the USA would train and equip, while US troops gradually came home.
US troop numbers fell from about 540,000 in 1969 to about 24,000 by the end of 1972. Conscription was replaced by a draft lottery (1969) and ended in 1973.
Weaknesses: the ARVN had low morale and high desertion rates, and its officers were often corrupt. Without US ground troops and air power it struggled.

sections.title: 2. Widening the war: Cambodia and Laos

blocks.p: To cut the Ho Chi Minh Trail and destroy communist bases, Nixon secretly bombed Cambodia from March 1969. In April 1970 US and ARVN troops invaded Cambodia. This caused huge protests in the USA, including at Kent State University, where National Guardsmen shot dead four students on 4 May 1970.
In February 1971 the ARVN invaded Laos (Operation Lam Son 719) with US air support but no US ground troops. It was a failure and showed the weakness of Vietnamisation.

In 1972 North Vietnam launched the Easter Offensive. Nixon responded with heavy bombing (Operation Linebacker), and in December 1972 the 'Christmas bombing' of Hanoi and Haiphong to push the North back to the negotiating table.

sections.title: 3. Peace talks and the Paris Peace Accords

blocks.p: Peace talks in Paris had begun in 1968. Henry Kissinger, Nixon's National Security Adviser, held secret talks with North Vietnam's Le Duc Tho. Nixon also improved relations with China and the USSR (visits in 1972), reducing their support for Hanoi.

The Paris Peace Accords were signed on 27 January 1973. There would be a ceasefire; US troops would leave within 60 days; prisoners of war would be returned; but North Vietnamese troops could stay in the South. The last US combat troops left in March 1973.

evidence: March 1973: last US combat troops leave.

blocks.p: The ceasefire soon broke down. Nixon resigned in August 1974 over Watergate. His successor Gerald Ford asked Congress for more aid for South Vietnam, but Congress refused; it had already cut aid and passed the War Powers Act (1973) limiting the President's power to send troops.

North Vietnam launched a final offensive in early 1975. The ARVN collapsed. Saigon fell on 30 April 1975 as the last Americans were evacuated by helicopter. Vietnam was reunified under communist rule in 1976, and Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City.

Reasons for US failure: the strengths of the North (determination, guerrilla tactics, the Ho Chi Minh Trail, support from China and the USSR); the weaknesses of the US military (tactics that turned peasants against them, low morale); the unpopular and corrupt South Vietnamese governments; and opposition to the war in the USA.

topics.title: Reactions to the war in the USA and Vietnam

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Historical investigation A4, key topic 5.

learn.intro: The war devastated Vietnamese civilians and divided American society. Media coverage, the draft and events such as My Lai fuelled a growing protest movement, while many Americans continued to support the war.

sections.title: 1. The impact of the war on civilians in Vietnam

blocks.p: More bombs were dropped on Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia than by all sides in the Second World War. Villages were destroyed by search and destroy missions, napalm and bombing. Millions of Vietnamese became refugees, many moving into crowded camps and the slums of Saigon.

Agent Orange destroyed crops and forests and caused cancers and birth defects for decades afterwards. Estimates of Vietnamese deaths vary widely, but they run into the millions, many of them civilians.
Civilians were also caught between both sides: the Vietcong used terror against officials and those who helped the government, as in the killings in Hue during Tet in 1968.

sections.title: 2. Opposition to the war in the USA

blocks.p: The anti-war movement grew from 1965. Students held 'teach-ins' and marches; Students for a Democratic Society (SDS) organised protests. Young men burned their draft cards; the draft hit poorer and Black Americans hardest. Martin Luther King Jr spoke against the war in 1967, and the boxer Muhammad Ali refused the draft.

The media was crucial: Vietnam was the first 'television war'. Images such as the Saigon police chief executing a Vietcong prisoner during Tet (1968) and reports of My Lai (published November 1969) shocked the public.

Protest peaked in 1969–71: huge Moratorium demonstrations in October and November 1969; Kent State (May 1970); veterans throwing away their medals in 1971; and the Pentagon Papers (1971) revealing that governments had misled the public.

sections.title: 3. Support for the war and the legacy

blocks.p: Not all Americans opposed the war. Many saw it as a fight against communism and saw protesters as unpatriotic. Nixon appealed to the 'silent majority' in November 1969. In May 1970 construction workers attacked anti-war students in New York (the 'Hard Hat Riot').

The war's legacy in the USA: about 58,000 Americans died; veterans often returned to a hostile or indifferent reception and many suffered long-term trauma; Congress passed the War Powers Act (1973) to limit the President's power to wage war; and trust in government fell.

learn.intro: How did Germany move from empire to democracy in 1918–19, and how did the new Weimar Republic survive crisis after crisis before enjoying its 'Golden Years'? Unit 1 essays often ask you to weigh the importance of one factor — Versailles, hyperinflation, Stresemann — against others.

sections.title: 1. Collapse of the Second Reich and creation of the Republic, 1918–19

blocks.p: The 'revolution from above': on 29 September 1918 Ludendorff and Hindenburg told the Kaiser the war was lost and urged a government based on the Reichstag majority, partly so that the civilian parties, not the army, would carry the blame for seeking peace. Prince Max of Baden became Chancellor in October and the October Reforms made the Chancellor responsible to the Reichstag.

The 'revolution from below': the naval mutiny at Kiel (late October–early November) spread into workers' and soldiers' councils across Germany; Bavaria was declared a republic on 7–8 November. On 9 November the Kaiser's abdication was announced, Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed a republic, and Friedrich Ebert (SPD) became Chancellor. The armistice followed on 11 November.

Ebert's priority was order. The Ebert–Groener pact (10 November) secured army support for the government against the radical left, and the Stinnes–Legien agreement (15 November) won employers' recognition of trade unions and the eight-hour day. Critics argue this left the old elites — army officers, judges, civil servants, industrialists — in place.

The Spartacist rising in Berlin (January 1919) was crushed by regular troops and Freikorps; Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht were murdered. Elections on 19 January 1919 gave the parties of the 'Weimar coalition' (SPD, Centre, DDP) about three-quarters of the vote. The National Assembly met at Weimar and the constitution was signed in August 1919.

evidence: January 1919: Spartacist rising crushed; Luxemburg and Liebknecht killed.
refs: Layton, From Kaiser to Führer, ch. 4 §3–4

sections.title: 2. The Weimar constitution and the parties

blocks.p: The constitution created a highly democratic system: a Reichstag elected every four years by proportional representation, with votes for men and women over 20; a President directly elected every seven years; a Chancellor appointed by the President but needing Reichstag support; a Reichsrat representing the states; and a long list of fundamental rights.

Its weaknesses are a classic essay theme. Proportional representation encouraged many small parties and short-lived coalitions. Article 48 let the President rule by emergency decree — used constructively by Ebert in 1923, but later by Hindenburg to bypass the Reichstag. The constitution left the old institutions of army, judiciary and civil service largely untouched.

ul: SPD — moderate socialists; largest party until July 1932; supported the Republic.
Centre (Zentrum) — Catholic party; in almost every coalition. BVP — its Bavarian sister party.
DDP — liberal democrats; strong in 1919, declined fast.
DVP — business-friendly liberals; Stresemann's party; accepted the Republic pragmatically.
DNVP — nationalists and monarchists; hostile to the Republic for most of the 1920s.
KPD — communists; sought a Soviet-style revolution. NSDAP — Hitler's party from 1920.

evidence: President elected every 7 years; Reichstag every 4.

blocks.p: The Treaty of Versailles (signed 28 June 1919) took about 13 per cent of Germany's European territory, including Alsace-Lorraine, Posen and West Prussia (the 'Polish corridor'), and later part of Upper Silesia; removed all colonies; limited the army to 100,000 men with no conscription, tanks or air force; demilitarised the Rhineland; and through Article 231 blamed Germany for the war. Reparations were fixed in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks. Many Germans called it a Diktat, and the 'stab-in-the-back' myth attached the defeat to the 'November criminals' who founded the Republic.

The extreme left: the Spartacist rising (January 1919), the Bavarian Soviet Republic (April–May 1919), the Ruhr workers' uprising after the Kapp Putsch (1920), the March Action (1921) and the Hamburg rising (October 1923). All were crushed, usually by the army and Freikorps.

The extreme right: the Kapp Putsch (March 1920) seized Berlin; the army would not fire on the rebels, but a general strike defeated it within days. Right-wing assassins killed Matthias Erzberger (1921) and Walther Rathenau (1922); of 376 political murders in 1919–22, 354 were committed by the right, and few killers were convicted. Hitler's Munich Putsch (November 1923) failed.

Hyperinflation: the war had been paid for by borrowing and printing money; reparations and budget deficits added pressure; the Franco-Belgian occupation of the Ruhr (January 1923) and the government's policy of paying striking workers for 'passive resistance' turned inflation into hyperinflation. By November 1923 one US dollar bought about 4.2 trillion marks. Savers, pensioners and those on fixed incomes lost most; debtors and some big industrialists gained.

Why did the Republic survive? Stresemann's 'hundred days' as Chancellor (August–November 1923) ended passive resistance and introduced the Rentenmark; the army stayed loyal against the left; Ebert used Article 48 decisively; its opponents were divided and badly organised; and the Dawes Plan (1924) brought foreign money. Historians debate whether survival owed more to the Republic's strengths or to its enemies' weaknesses.

sections.title: 4. The 'Golden Years', 1924–29

blocks.p: Gustav Stresemann, Foreign Minister from 1923 until his death in October 1929, pursued 'fulfilment': co-operating with the Allies to win revisions. The Dawes Plan (1924) rescheduled reparations and brought American loans; the Locarno Treaties (1925) accepted Germany's western borders; Germany joined the League of Nations in 1926; it signed the Kellogg–Briand Pact (1928); and the Young Plan (1929) reduced the total owed and promised early Allied withdrawal from the Rhineland.

Paul von Hindenburg was elected President in 1925 after Ebert's death. A monarchist war hero, he acted constitutionally in the 1920s, which reassured conservatives — but his election also showed how far German voters still looked to the old order.

Prosperity rested on foreign loans, especially from the USA, a stable currency and rationalisation of industry; industrial production regained its pre-war level by 1928. Social reforms extended the welfare state, including unemployment insurance (1927), and house-building expanded. Women had the vote and constitutional equality, and more worked in offices and shops, though traditional attitudes stayed strong.

Underlying weaknesses remained. Unemployment never fell below about 1.3 million; agriculture was in depression from the late 1920s, with falling prices and rising debt; the economy depended on short-term American loans; coalitions remained fragile; and the DNVP and Nazis stayed hostile. The 'Golden Years' are often described as stability on the surface rather than real strength.

evidence: Dawes Plan 1924; Locarno 1925; League of Nations 1926; Kellogg–Briand 1928; Young Plan 1929.
Unemployment never fell below about 1.3 million.

sections.title: 5. Weimar culture

blocks.p: The relaxation of censorship and the energy of Berlin produced remarkable culture. Expressionist and 'New Objectivity' (Neue Sachlichkeit) artists such as Otto Dix and George Grosz painted war-wounded veterans, profiteers and city life with savage realism.

German cinema was among the most innovative in the world: The Cabinet of Dr Caligari (1920) and Fritz Lang's Metropolis (1927). In theatre, Bertolt Brecht and Kurt Weill's The Threepenny Opera (1928) mocked bourgeois society. The Bauhaus, founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919 and moved to Dessau in 1925, combined art, craft and industrial design.

Culture divided opinion. To many conservatives and Nazis it was 'decadent' and 'un-German' — evidence that the Republic was undermining traditional values. Its significance in essays is often how it widened the gap between modern urban Germany and conservative, rural and religious Germany.

evidence: The Cabinet of Dr Caligari (1920); Metropolis (1927).

learn.intro: From a tiny Munich party in 1919 to government in 1933: why did the Nazis fail in the 1920s, break through after 1929, and how did Hitler — who never won a majority in a free election — become Chancellor?

blocks.p: The German Workers' Party (DAP) was founded in Munich in January 1919 by Anton Drexler. Hitler, then an army political informant, joined in September 1919 and quickly became its star speaker. In February 1920 the party announced its 25-point programme — nationalist, anti-Semitic, anti-Versailles and vaguely anti-capitalist — and renamed itself the National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP).

In July 1921 Hitler became party leader with near-total authority. The SA (Sturmabteilung) grew from the party's stewards in 1921; Ernst Röhm, an army officer with links to the Bavarian authorities and Freikorps, was vital in building it into a paramilitary force. The party bought its own newspaper, the Völkischer Beobachter, in 1920.

The Munich (Beer Hall) Putsch of 8–9 November 1923 tried to exploit the crisis year, copying Mussolini's march on Rome. Hitler counted on the Bavarian leaders Kahr, Lossow and Seisser, but they turned against him; the march through Munich was dispersed by police gunfire and 16 Nazis were killed. The failure taught Hitler that power would have to be won through the system.

sections.title: 2. Failure and survival, 1924–28

blocks.p: Hitler's trial (February–March 1924) gave him national publicity, and sympathetic judges gave him a five-year sentence of which he served about nine months in Landsberg prison. There he wrote Mein Kampf, setting out his ideas on race, Lebensraum and leadership, and decided on the 'legal path' to power.

The party was refounded in February 1925. At the Bamberg Conference (February 1926) Hitler defeated the northern, more socialist wing led by Gregor Strasser, establishing the Führerprinzip and his control of the programme. Joseph Goebbels switched to Hitler's side and became Gauleiter of Berlin.

A national organisation developed: regional Gaue, the Hitler Youth (1926), the SS as a personal bodyguard, and specialist groups for farmers, students and professions. But in the stable conditions of the mid-1920s the party struggled: in the Reichstag election of May 1928 it won only 2.6 per cent and 12 seats. It began to shift attention to rural, Protestant northern Germany, where agricultural depression was already hurting.

evidence: Sentence of 5 years; served about 9 months.

blocks.p: In 1929 the Nazis joined Alfred Hugenberg's DNVP and other nationalists in a campaign against the Young Plan. The referendum failed, but Hugenberg's newspapers gave Hitler national publicity and respectability with the conservative right.

The Wall Street Crash (October 1929) led American lenders to recall loans. German industrial output fell sharply and unemployment reached 6.1 million by January 1932. The Grand Coalition collapsed in March 1930 over unemployment-insurance contributions; Heinrich Brüning's government then governed increasingly through Article 48 decrees, and his deflationary cuts deepened the misery.

The Nazi vote rose to 18.3 per cent (107 seats) in September 1930 and 37.3 per cent (230 seats, the largest party) in July 1932. Goebbels's propaganda, mass rallies, Hitler's flights across Germany in 1932 and targeted messages to farmers, the middle classes and young voters were combined with SA intimidation and street violence. The Nazis drew support from across society, though most heavily from Protestant, rural and middle-class Germany.

The Communist vote also grew — reaching 16.9 per cent and 100 seats in November 1932 — which frightened the middle classes, industrialists and the elites, and made the Nazis look like the barrier against Bolshevism. In the Reichstag, Nazis and Communists together formed a negative majority that made parliamentary government almost impossible.

sections.title: 4. Coming to power, November 1932–March 1933

blocks.p: Hindenburg had replaced Brüning with Franz von Papen (June 1932), who lifted the ban on the SA and called the July election. Hitler refused anything less than the chancellorship. In November 1932 the Nazi vote fell to 33.1 per cent (196 seats), funds were low and the party seemed to have peaked.

General Kurt von Schleicher became Chancellor in December 1932 and tried to split the Nazis by offering Gregor Strasser the vice-chancellorship. Papen, seeking revenge, met Hitler in January 1933 and persuaded Hindenburg that a cabinet with Hitler as Chancellor, but only three Nazis, could be controlled by conservatives. Hitler was appointed on 30 January 1933.

Hitler then used state power to win support and crush opponents. On 3 February he reassured army leaders; on 20 February leading industrialists pledged money for the election campaign. Göring, as Prussian Interior Minister, enrolled SA and SS men as auxiliary police. After the Reichstag Fire (27 February), blamed on the Communist Marinus van der Lubbe, the Decree for the Protection of the People and the State (28 February) suspended civil liberties. In the election of 5 March the Nazis won 43.9 per cent (288 seats) — still not a majority without the DNVP.

The historians' debate: was Hitler's appointment the product of Nazi popularity and propaganda, of the economic crisis, of the structural weaknesses of Weimar, or — the most common emphasis — of the 'backstairs intrigue' of a small group of conservatives around Hindenburg who thought they could use him?

evidence: 30 January 1933: Hitler appointed; three Nazis in cabinet.
27–28 February 1933: Reichstag Fire and emergency decree.

flashcards.q: What were Brüning's economic policies and their effect?
flashcards.a: Deflation — spending and wage cuts — which deepened unemployment and earned him the name 'hunger chancellor'.

flashcards.q: Give three Nazi methods of winning support 1930–32.
flashcards.a: Goebbels's propaganda; mass rallies and Hitler's flights; targeted messages to groups; SA marches and intimidation.

flashcards.q: Which groups voted Nazi most heavily?
flashcards.a: Protestant, rural and middle-class Germans; but support came from across society.

flashcards.q: What was Schleicher's plan in December 1932?
flashcards.a: To split the Nazis by offering Gregor Strasser a post and win union support — it failed.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q:
Historians differ in their judgements about why Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933.
‘Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933 mainly because of the political intrigue of the conservative elites.’
Assess this view using your own knowledge of the issue.

model.t: In line with my judgement, the intrigue of the conservative elites was the decisive reason. In November 1932 the Nazi vote had fallen to 33.1 per cent and the party was short of money; it was Papen's meeting with Hitler in January 1933 and his persuasion of Hindenburg that turned a declining movement into a government.
model.n: Most important factor: point linked to the judgement + precise evidence (statistic, people, date).

model.t: A dissenting view might point to the 37.3 per cent won in July 1932, arguing that without mass support no conservative would have considered Hitler at all.

On the balance however, mass support gave Hitler a claim to power but not power itself: Hindenburg refused him the chancellorship in August 1932 despite that result. Judged by effectiveness, only the elites could make the appointment. Thus we must assert that intrigue was the most important reason.
model.n: Why it still wins + criterion + sustained judgement.

learn.intro: How did the Nazis turn an appointment as Chancellor into a dictatorship within 18 months, how did they control and shape German society, and how successful were their economic policies? This key topic produces many Unit 1 questions.

sections.title: 1. Establishing the dictatorship, 1933–34

blocks.p: The Enabling Act (23 March 1933) let the government make laws without the Reichstag for four years. It passed by 444 votes to 94: Communist deputies were already arrested or in hiding, SA men surrounded the building, and the Centre Party voted in favour after promises about the Catholic Church. Only the SPD voted against.

Gleichschaltung (coordination) followed. The federal states were placed under Reich governors (April 1933) and their parliaments abolished (January 1934). Trade unions were broken up on 2 May 1933 and replaced by the German Labour Front (DAF). The SPD was banned in June, other parties dissolved themselves, and on 14 July 1933 the Nazis became the only legal party.

The SA, now millions strong, wanted a 'second revolution' and Röhm hoped to merge it with the army. The army and big business were alarmed. In the Night of the Long Knives (30 June–2 July 1934) the SS murdered Röhm and other SA leaders, along with old enemies such as Schleicher, Gregor Strasser and Kahr. The army was reassured and the SS became the regime's main instrument of terror.

When Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934, Hitler merged the offices of Chancellor and President as Führer. The army swore a personal oath of loyalty to Hitler, and a plebiscite on 19 August approved the change with about 90 per cent of the vote.

evidence: 30 June–2 July 1934: Night of the Long Knives.
2 August 1934: Hindenburg dies; army oath to Hitler.

sections.title: 2. The nature of Nazi government, 1934–39

blocks.p: Hitler's style of government was unusual. He disliked routine paperwork, spent long periods at his Bavarian retreat, and the cabinet met less and less, last meeting in 1938. Decisions were often given orally and many ministers rarely saw him.

Power was spread between competing agencies — ministries, party offices, the SS, and special plenipotentiaries such as Göring for the Four-Year Plan. Historians call this polycracy. Intentionalist historians see Hitler deliberately dividing to rule; structuralists see a chaotic system in which officials competed by 'working towards the Führer' (Ian Kershaw's phrase), radicalising policy.

The 'dual state' (Ernst Fraenkel, 1941): a 'normative state' of ordinary laws and courts continued to operate for most everyday matters, alongside a 'prerogative state' — the party, SS and police — which acted outside the law whenever the regime chose.

evidence: Göring made plenipotentiary for the Four-Year Plan (1936).

sections.title: 3. Repression and control

blocks.p: Heinrich Himmler built the terror apparatus. He took control of the political police across the states in 1934 and became Chief of the German Police in June 1936, uniting the police with the SS. The Gestapo (secret state police) and the SD (the SS intelligence service under Reinhard Heydrich) watched for opponents. The first concentration camp opened at Dachau in March 1933, and thousands were held in 'protective custody'.
The Gestapo was small. Research on local records shows it relied heavily on denunciations from ordinary Germans, whose motives ranged from loyalty to personal grudges. Fear and consent overlapped.

Joseph Goebbels's Ministry of Popular Enlightenment and Propaganda (March 1933) and the Reich Chamber of Culture (September 1933) controlled the press, radio, film and the arts. Cheap 'People's Receiver' radios, the Nuremberg rallies, the 1936 Berlin Olympics and films such as Triumph of the Will (1935) spread the Hitler myth.

Opposition and dissent were limited and fragmented: underground SPD and KPD cells were broken up; the Confessing Church (Pastor Martin Niemöller) resisted Nazi control of the Protestant Church; some young people rejected the Hitler Youth; army officers plotted in 1938. Much dissent was 'non-conformity' — grumbling, listening to foreign radio, avoiding the Hitler salute — rather than active resistance.

evidence: June 1936: Himmler Chief of the German Police.
1935: Triumph of the Will; 1936: Berlin Olympics.

sections.title: 4. Shaping society: the Volksgemeinschaft

blocks.p: The Volksgemeinschaft (people's community) was meant to replace class and religious division with racial unity and loyalty to the Führer. It was built by including 'racially valuable' Germans and excluding everyone else.

Women: Kinder, Küche, Kirche. Marriage loans (1933) were reduced for each child born; the Mother's Cross (1938) rewarded large families; women were pushed out of the higher civil service, law and medicine. Yet the demands of rearmament meant women's employment rose in the later 1930s. The Nazi women's organisations were led by Gertrud Scholtz-Klink.

Workers: Robert Ley's German Labour Front (DAF) replaced unions. Its subsidiaries Strength through Joy (KdF) offered cheap holidays, sport and the Volkswagen savings scheme, and Beauty of Labour improved workplaces — compensation for longer hours and frozen wages.

Youth and education: teachers had to join the Nazi Teachers' League; the curriculum emphasised race, history and physical education. The Hitler Youth and League of German Maidens became the official youth organisations in 1936, with membership made compulsory in 1939.

Racial policy and the churches: the sterilisation law (July 1933), the boycott of Jewish shops (1 April 1933) and the exclusion of Jews from the civil service (April 1933), the Nuremberg Laws (September 1935) and the Kristallnacht pogrom (9–10 November 1938) escalated persecution. The Concordat with the Vatican (July 1933) was soon broken; the Pope's encyclical 'With Burning Concern' (1937) criticised the regime.

evidence: 1 April 1933: boycott; September 1935: Nuremberg Laws; 9–10 November 1938: Kristallnacht.
1936: Hitler Youth the official youth organisation; 1939: compulsory.

sections.title: 5. Economic policies

blocks.p: Hjalmar Schacht (Reichsbank President from 1933, Economics Minister 1934–37) financed recovery and rearmament through deficit spending and Mefo bills, which hid the cost of rearmament. His New Plan (1934) controlled imports and made bilateral trade deals, especially with south-eastern Europe.

Unemployment fell from about 6 million in early 1933 to well under half a million by 1939, helped by public works such as the autobahns, the Reich Labour Service, conscription (from 1935), rearmament and statistical tricks that removed women and Jews from the figures.

In 1936 Göring's Four-Year Plan aimed to make Germany ready for war within four years through autarky — synthetic oil and rubber, and state-run industries such as the Hermann Göring Works. Schacht, who warned about the cost, resigned in 1937. Most targets were missed.

Living standards: jobs returned, but real wages only slowly recovered to late-1920s levels, hours were longer and food choice was limited ('guns or butter'). Farmers were promised protection through the Reich Food Estate and the Reich Entailed Farm Law (1933), but the drift from the land continued.

evidence: Schacht resigned as Economics Minister in 1937.

learn.intro: How did Nazi Germany organise its economy and control its people at war, how did the war become a racial war of genocide, and why did Germany lose? Questions here often ask you to weigh one reason — bombing, Speer, Hitler's mistakes — against others.

sections.title: 1. Managing the war economy

blocks.p: Germany went to war short of oil, rubber and many metals, short of labour once millions were conscripted, and short of motor transport — the army that invaded the USSR in 1941 still relied heavily on horses. Production in 1939–41 was hampered by competing agencies, over-engineered weapons and the armed services' demands for custom designs.

Fritz Todt became Minister of Armaments in 1940. After his death in a plane crash in February 1942, Albert Speer took over. Speer centralised planning, standardised designs, let industrialists run production committees and used mass-production methods; armaments output roughly tripled between early 1942 and mid-1944, despite bombing.

Göring, as head of the Four-Year Plan and the Luftwaffe, lost influence through failures and inefficiency. Labour shortages were met above all with foreign workers and prisoners — about 7 million by 1944, many forced labourers treated brutally — rather than by fully mobilising German women, whom the regime was reluctant to conscript.

German technological ingenuity was real — jet aircraft, the V-1 and V-2 rockets, synthetic fuel — but it often came too late, in too small numbers, or diverted scarce resources from weapons that could be mass-produced.

evidence: Todt Armaments Minister 1940–February 1942; Speer from February 1942.
Armaments output roughly tripled between 1942 and mid-1944.
About 7 million foreign workers and prisoners by 1944.

blocks.p: Rationing began in August 1939. Living standards were cushioned in the early war years by plunder from occupied Europe, but rations were cut in 1942 and conditions worsened sharply as defeats mounted.

Allied bombing intensified from 1942. The raids on Hamburg in July 1943 killed around 40,000 people; Dresden was devastated in February 1945. Millions of homes were destroyed and many civilians evacuated. Bombing hurt morale but did not produce the collapse the Allies hoped for.

Goebbels sustained morale through radio, newsreels and films, and after Stalingrad proclaimed 'total war' in his Sportpalast speech of February 1943. Himmler, Interior Minister from August 1943, intensified repression: the People's Court handed down death sentences in rising numbers, and defeatism could be punished by death.

Opposition grew but remained small and divided: the White Rose students in Munich (the Scholls, executed in 1943); the Edelweiss Pirates, some of whom were hanged in Cologne in 1944; Bishop von Galen's 1941 sermons against the murder of disabled people; the conservative Kreisau Circle; and the army officers' July Bomb Plot (20 July 1944), led by Stauffenberg, after which thousands were arrested and around 200 executed in direct connection.

The conquest of Poland in 1939 brought about two million Jews under German rule. Himmler was made responsible for 'strengthening Germandom' — resettling ethnic Germans and expelling Poles and Jews. Jews were forced into ghettos such as Łódź and Warsaw (1940), where many died of starvation and disease.

The invasion of the USSR (June 1941) was planned as a racial war of annihilation. Einsatzgruppen — SS mobile killing units — and police battalions shot Jews, communists and others in mass executions; hundreds of thousands were murdered in the first months, and millions of Soviet prisoners of war died of hunger and neglect.

From late 1941 the regime moved to systematic murder by gas. The Wannsee Conference (20 January 1942), chaired by Heydrich, co-ordinated the 'Final Solution' across government agencies. Death camps — Chelmno, Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau — murdered millions. About six million Jews were killed in the Holocaust, along with Roma, disabled people and others.

Historians debate whether genocide followed Hitler's long-held intention or evolved through 'cumulative radicalisation' as competing agencies, the war in the east and local initiatives escalated policy. Most now combine both: Hitler's ideology set the goal, the conditions of war shaped the timing and methods.

sections.title: 4. Losing the war

blocks.p: Balance of resources: once the USSR (June 1941) and the USA (December 1941) were at war with Germany, the Allies had far greater manpower, raw materials and industrial capacity. American and Soviet production of tanks and aircraft outstripped Germany's even at Speer's peak.

Sea power: Allied navies blockaded Germany and kept Britain supplied. The U-boat campaign was defeated in the Battle of the Atlantic by May 1943, allowing American troops and supplies to cross for the invasions of Italy and France.

Bombing: strategic bombing destroyed cities, transport and, in 1944, synthetic-oil plants. It also forced Germany to divert huge resources — fighters, anti-aircraft guns and soldiers — to air defence, a 'second front' in the air.

Hitler's strategic mistakes: invading the USSR before defeating Britain; declaring war on the USA on 11 December 1941; refusing to allow retreats, most famously at Stalingrad, where the Sixth Army surrendered in February 1943; and diverting resources to prestige projects. Hitler killed himself on 30 April 1945 and Germany surrendered on 7–8 May.

evidence: 11 December 1941: Germany declares war on the USA.
May 1943: U-boats withdrawn from the North Atlantic.
30 April 1945: Hitler's suicide; 8 May 1945: VE Day.

learn.intro: China moved from imperial collapse through warlord chaos, Guomindang rule and civil war to Mao's communist 'new dynasty'. Unit 2 essays often ask whether one factor or one period was the most significant cause of disorder — or how far Mao's control was ever secure.

sections.title: 1. The downfall of the Qing and resulting chaos, 1900–27

blocks.p: Reformers and revolutionaries: after the Boxer disaster the Qing tried late reforms — the traditional civil-service examinations were abolished in 1905 and provincial assemblies were promised. But reform raised expectations it could not meet. Revolutionaries led by Sun Yat-sen formed the Tongmenghui (Revolutionary Alliance) in 1905.

The 1911–12 revolution began with an army mutiny at Wuchang on 10 October 1911; province after province declared independence. Sun Yat-sen became provisional President, but the military strongman Yuan Shikai negotiated the abdication of the child emperor Puyi (February 1912) and took the presidency himself.

The failure of Yuan Shikai: he crushed the Guomindang (GMD) after its election success (its leader Song Jiaoren was assassinated in 1913), accepted most of Japan's 21 Demands (1915), and declared himself emperor in December 1915. Provinces revolted, he abandoned the monarchy, and he died in June 1916.
The warlord era (1916–28): regional military leaders controlled their own areas, taxed peasants heavily and fought each other; the central government in Beijing had little real power.

The May 4th Movement (1919): students protested in Beijing when the Treaty of Versailles gave Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan. It became a wider movement against Confucian tradition and for science and democracy, and inspired many future communists. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) was founded in 1921.

Sun Yat-sen and the GMD in the 1920s: Sun's Three Principles of the People were nationalism, democracy and people's livelihood. With Soviet help he reorganised the GMD, formed the First United Front with the CCP (1923–24) and set up the Whampoa Military Academy (1924) under Chiang Kai-shek. Sun died in March 1925.

evidence: December 1915: Yuan declares himself emperor; dies June 1916.

sections.title: 2. Chiang Kai-shek and the attempt to restore order, 1927–49

blocks.p: Emergence of Chiang and the break with the Communists: Chiang led the Northern Expedition (from 1926) against the warlords. In April 1927 he turned on his allies, massacring Communists and union members in Shanghai. The GMD set up a national government at Nanjing in 1928, though many warlords only nominally accepted it.
The Communists retreated to rural bases such as the Jiangxi Soviet. Chiang launched five encirclement campaigns (1930–34); the fifth, using blockhouses and blockade, forced the CCP to break out.

The Long March (October 1934 – October 1935): roughly 80,000–90,000 set out from Jiangxi; fewer than 10,000 reached Shaanxi in the north-west. At the Zunyi Conference (January 1935) Mao Zedong gained a leading role. The March was a military disaster but became a powerful propaganda legend, and the CCP survived.

The failure to crush the Communists: in the Xi'an Incident (December 1936) Chiang was kidnapped by his own commander Zhang Xueliang and forced into a Second United Front against Japan. During the war the CCP grew from its Yan'an base through guerrilla warfare, moderate land policies and discipline.

The civil war 1946–49 and its outcome: despite US aid, the GMD lost. Reasons include GMD corruption and hyperinflation, the damage of the war against Japan, poor generalship, CCP land reform winning peasant support, CCP discipline and morale, captured Japanese weapons in Manchuria, and decisive campaigns such as Huaihai (1948–49). Mao proclaimed the People's Republic on 1 October 1949; Chiang fled to Taiwan.

Establishing communist control 1949–57: land reform (1950–52) gave land to peasants and destroyed the landlord class, with mass 'speak bitterness' meetings and very many killings. The Three Antis and Five Antis campaigns (1951–52) targeted corruption among officials and businessmen. The campaign against counter-revolutionaries and the Korean War atmosphere tightened control.

The Hundred Flowers Campaign (1956–57): Mao invited criticism — 'let a hundred flowers bloom'. Intellectuals criticised the Party sharply. In June 1957 it was replaced by the Anti-Rightist Campaign, in which hundreds of thousands were labelled 'rightists' and many were sent to labour camps. Historians debate whether it was a trap or a genuine invitation that went wrong.

The Chairman and his critics: Peng Dehuai criticised the Great Leap Forward at the Lushan Conference (1959) and was purged. After the famine, Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping led recovery from 1962 and Mao stepped back. Lin Biao built Mao's cult in the army (the Little Red Book, 1964). Mao launched the Cultural Revolution (1966) to regain control: Liu died in custody (1969) and Deng was sent to work in a tractor factory.

Supporters and survivors: Lin Biao was named Mao's successor in 1969 but died in a plane crash in September 1971 after an alleged coup plot. Zhou Enlai survived every purge and managed government and diplomacy until his death in January 1976. Jiang Qing (Mao's wife) led the radical Gang of Four. Mao died on 9 September 1976; the Gang of Four were arrested a month later.

misconceptions.right: Power passed to Yuan Shikai and then to warlords; China fragmented.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence that the downfall of the Qing led to chaos.
evidence.model: After Puyi abdicated in 1912, Yuan Shikai crushed the GMD and tried to become emperor (1915); after his death in 1916 the warlord era fragmented China until 1928.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence that Mao's control was challenged after 1959.
evidence.model: Peng Dehuai attacked the Great Leap at Lushan (1959); after 1962 Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping ran recovery policies while Mao stepped back.

flashcards.a: He crushed parliament, accepted most of the 21 Demands and tried to become emperor (1915); provinces revolted and he died in 1916.

flashcards.q: Why was the May 4th Movement significant?
flashcards.a: Nationalist anger at Versailles; attack on Confucian tradition; inspired the founding generation of the CCP.

flashcards.q: Why was the Long March significant?
flashcards.a: The CCP survived; Mao rose (Zunyi 1935); it became a legend of heroism for propaganda.

flashcards.q: Why did the CCP win the civil war?
flashcards.a: GMD corruption and hyperinflation; war damage; CCP land reform and peasant support; discipline; Manchurian weapons; good generalship.
Land reform, Three/Five Antis, campaigns against counter-revolutionaries, Anti-Rightist Campaign.

flashcards.q: Why did Mao launch the Cultural Revolution?
flashcards.a: To regain power from Liu and Deng, purge 'capitalist roaders' and renew revolutionary spirit.

topics.title: The impact of the world on China, 1900–76

review.note: Original content following the IAL specification (Issue 6), Option 1B key topic 2. Figures to be checked against class resources.

learn.intro: From the humiliation of the Boxer Protocol to Nixon's handshake with Mao, outside powers shaped China's politics and its sense of itself. Essays ask about change over time: was China always a victim, or did it learn to use the great powers?

sections.title: 1. Weakness and humiliation, 1900–19

blocks.p: The Boxer Rising (1899–1901) — origins: the Boxers (Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists) were a peasant movement in Shandong, angered by foreign concessions, Christian missionaries and converts, and drought and floods that brought hunger. Their slogan became 'Support the Qing, destroy the foreigners'.

Impact: in June 1900 the Boxers besieged the foreign legations in Beijing and the Empress Dowager Cixi declared war on the foreign powers. An Eight-Nation Alliance relieved the legations in August 1900 and looted Beijing. The Boxer Protocol (September 1901) imposed a huge indemnity of 450 million taels and allowed foreign troops in Beijing. The Qing were humiliated, which pushed them into late reforms and strengthened revolutionaries.

British power in Shanghai and the Yangtze: Britain dominated the Shanghai International Settlement, controlled much trade and shipping in the Yangtze Valley, and ran the Chinese Maritime Customs. Foreigners had extraterritoriality — they were tried in their own courts, not Chinese ones.

Japan and the 21 Demands (January 1915): with the European powers busy in the First World War, Japan demanded control of Shandong, rights in Manchuria, and (in a final group of demands) Japanese advisers in the Chinese government. Yuan Shikai accepted most of them in May 1915, except the last group. At Versailles (1919), Germany's Shandong rights were given to Japan, triggering the May 4th Movement.

evidence: 1919: Versailles gives Shandong rights to Japan.

blocks.p: Origins and impact of the Manchurian crisis (1931–33): Japan had railway and economic interests in Manchuria and wanted its resources. On 18 September 1931 Japanese officers staged an explosion on the South Manchuria Railway near Mukden and used it as an excuse to occupy Manchuria. In 1932 Japan created the puppet state of Manchukuo with Puyi as head. The League of Nations' Lytton Report condemned Japan, which left the League in 1933. The Tanggu Truce (May 1933) confirmed Japanese control.
Chiang's policy of 'first internal pacification, then external resistance' — fighting the Communists before Japan — was unpopular and led to the Xi'an Incident (1936).

Full-scale war from 1937: a clash at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing on 7 July 1937 escalated into all-out war. Japan took Shanghai after heavy fighting and captured Nanjing in December 1937, where its troops committed a massacre of civilians and prisoners. The GMD moved its capital to Chongqing.

Initial Japanese success came from a modern army, air power and control of the coast. By 1938–39 there was stalemate: Japan held the cities and railways but could not control the vast interior, and the CCP built guerrilla bases behind Japanese lines.

The role of the USA: after Pearl Harbor (December 1941) the USA supplied the GMD by air over 'the Hump' and the Burma Road, sent General Stilwell as Chiang's chief of staff, and recognised China as one of the 'Big Four'. Friction between Stilwell and Chiang, and US frustration at GMD corruption, grew.

sections.title: 3. The impact on China of the Cold War

blocks.p: The Soviet alliance: Mao visited Moscow and signed the Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship (February 1950). The USSR provided loans, thousands of advisers and help with around 150 major industrial projects, which were central to the First Five-Year Plan (1953–57).

The Korean War (1950–53): when UN forces approached the Yalu River, China sent the Chinese People's Volunteers (October 1950). Losses were very heavy — Mao's own son was killed — but China fought the USA to a standstill, gaining prestige. At home the war justified mass campaigns against 'counter-revolutionaries'. The US Seventh Fleet now protected Taiwan, ending hopes of taking it.

Origins of the Sino-Soviet split: Khrushchev's 1956 'secret speech' attacking Stalin and his policy of peaceful coexistence; Soviet criticism of the Great Leap Forward; disputes over nuclear help; and rivalry for leadership of world communism. In 1960 the USSR withdrew its advisers, leaving projects unfinished. Border clashes on the Ussuri River (Zhenbao Island, March 1969) raised fears of war.

Impact and the beginnings of détente: fearing the USSR, China turned to the West. 'Ping-pong diplomacy' (April 1971) was followed by Kissinger's secret visit (July 1971), China's admission to the UN in place of Taiwan (October 1971) and President Nixon's visit in February 1972 (the Shanghai Communiqué). Other Western statesmen, such as British Prime Minister Edward Heath (1974), followed.

evidence: October 1950: China enters the Korean War.

learn.intro: China's economy grew in patches before 1949 — railways, Shanghai's mills, Japanese Manchuria — but war and civil strife held it back. Mao then tried to force the pace, with Soviet-style planning, the disaster of the Great Leap Forward, recovery and renewed chaos.

blocks.p: Improving communications: railways expanded rapidly, often built with foreign loans and control — for example the Beijing–Hankou line (completed 1906). Railways moved goods and troops faster and linked inland areas to ports, but foreign ownership caused resentment: protests over railway nationalisation helped spark the 1911 revolution.
The telegraph linked cities and allowed faster government and business communication — and the rapid spread of news, for example during the 1911 revolution.
River traffic: steamships on the Yangtze and other rivers, many foreign-owned, carried most bulk trade. Rivers remained cheaper for heavy goods than rail, so historians debate which mattered more.

Native industry: during the First World War European imports fell, giving Chinese-owned cotton mills and flour mills a 'golden age' of growth. Shanghai became China's main industrial and financial centre, with foreign and Chinese factories, banks and a growing working class — which made it a centre of labour protest in the 1920s.

Industry in Japanese-controlled Manchuria: Japan invested heavily in Manchukuo — coal, steel (for example at Anshan), railways and power. By the late 1930s Manchuria was the most industrialised part of China, but it served Japan's war economy, not Chinese needs.

T. V. Soong, finance minister for the Nanjing government, set up the Central Bank of China (1928), won back control over tariffs from the foreign powers, and tried to balance the budget. The China Development Finance Corporation (1934) was meant to channel investment into industry and infrastructure. Successes were limited: military spending on the anti-communist campaigns swallowed most revenue.

The negative impact of war and civil strife: the Japanese invasion from 1937 destroyed much coastal industry and cut the GMD off from its tax base. Printing money to pay for war caused hyperinflation in the 1940s; the gold yuan currency introduced in 1948 collapsed within months. Peasants suffered heavy taxes, conscription and famine (for example in Henan in 1942–43).

sections.title: 3. Forcing the pace, 1949–76

blocks.p: Collectivisation: after land reform gave peasants land, the Party moved them step by step into mutual aid teams, then cooperatives, then larger collectives by 1956–57. The First Five-Year Plan (1953–57), with Soviet help, focused on heavy industry; steel, coal and electricity output rose sharply, though agriculture lagged.

The Great Leap Forward (1958–62): Mao aimed to overtake Britain's industrial output within 15 years. Peasants were organised into huge people's communes with communal kitchens; millions worked on backyard furnaces producing mostly useless iron; Lysenko-inspired farming methods such as close planting failed. Officials, fearful after the Anti-Rightist Campaign, reported fictional harvests, so grain was taken from starving villages.

Consequences: the famine of 1959–61 killed tens of millions — estimates range from about 15 million to over 40 million. Industry and agriculture were badly damaged and the Sino-Soviet split removed aid. Peng Dehuai's criticism at Lushan (1959) was punished, which prolonged the disaster.

Recovery and chaos 1962–76: Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping allowed private plots, rural markets and material incentives — Deng's phrase that it does not matter whether a cat is black or white, so long as it catches mice. Output recovered. The Cultural Revolution (from 1966) disrupted industry and transport, especially in 1966–68, and the 'Third Front' moved industry inland for defence at great cost. The economy grew in the 1970s but remained poor and inefficient.

evidence: 1959–61: famine — estimates from about 15 to over 40 million deaths.

learn.intro: Women's lives, health, education, belief and culture all changed between 1900 and 1976 — first through Western influence and the May 4th generation, then through the Communist regime's campaigns. Essays often ask how far change reached the countryside, or how significant one reform was.

sections.title: 1. The changing status of women

blocks.p: Early 20th century: Western ideas, missionary schools and girls' education spread new views. Anti-foot-binding societies grew, and the new Republic discouraged the practice after 1912, though it continued in rural areas for years. The May 4th generation attacked arranged marriages and Confucian rules that made women subordinate to fathers and husbands.

The Communist regime 1949–66: the Marriage Law of 1 May 1950 banned arranged marriages, child marriage, concubinage and the sale of brides, and gave women the right to divorce and to own property. Many women used it to escape bad marriages — divorce cases rose sharply in the early 1950s — but there was violent resistance in some villages, and many women were killed or took their own lives in disputes.

Patterns of change 1950–76: women joined the workforce in large numbers, especially during the Great Leap Forward, and Mao's slogan said 'women hold up half the sky'. But women usually earned fewer work points, still did most housework, and were rare in senior Party posts. Change was much faster in cities than in the countryside, where traditional family structures persisted.

evidence: Divorce cases rose sharply in the early 1950s.

blocks.p: Early 20th century: missionaries founded schools, universities and hospitals that spread Western medicine and educational ideas; the Rockefeller-funded Peking Union Medical College opened in 1917. The abolition of the imperial examinations (1905) opened the way to modern schools. But provision was concentrated in cities and coastal areas.

Growth of literacy after 1949: mass literacy campaigns, winter schools for peasants, simplified characters (from 1956) and pinyin romanisation (1958) helped literacy rise substantially. Education was used for political indoctrination, and the Cultural Revolution closed universities from 1966, with entrance exams not restored until after Mao's death.

Health: Patriotic Health Campaigns attacked disease through mass sanitation and the 'Four Pests' campaign (1958) — killing sparrows contributed to insect damage to crops. From 1965 Mao demanded more rural healthcare, and 'barefoot doctors' — peasants with a few months' training — gave basic treatment, vaccinations and hygiene advice. Life expectancy rose sharply between 1949 and 1976. Failures: limited training, shortages of medicine, and the famine of 1959–61.

sections.title: 3. Cultural and religious change

blocks.p: Christianity spread through missionary schools, hospitals and converts in the early 20th century; leading figures such as Sun Yat-sen and Chiang Kai-shek were Christians. Marxism spread after the Russian Revolution and May 4th; the CCP was founded in 1921.

The May 4th generation and the New Culture Movement (e.g. Chen Duxiu's magazine New Youth) rejected Confucian thought as the cause of China's weakness, calling for 'Mr Science and Mr Democracy' and writing in vernacular Chinese.
American culture influenced cities like Shanghai in the 1930s and 40s — Hollywood films, jazz, fashion and consumer goods — alongside a lively Chinese film and publishing industry.

Attacks on religion under the Communists: foreign missionaries were expelled in the early 1950s, churches were placed under state-controlled bodies such as the Three-Self Patriotic Movement, Buddhist and Daoist institutions were restricted, and Tibet was occupied in 1950, with the Dalai Lama fleeing in 1959.

The Cultural Revolution 1966–76 and its significance: Red Guards attacked the 'Four Olds' (old customs, culture, habits and ideas), destroying temples, books and art and persecuting teachers and intellectuals. Jiang Qing allowed only a few 'model operas'. From 1968 millions of urban youth were sent 'up to the mountains and down to the countryside'. Its significance: a 'lost generation' of education, deep distrust of the Party, and the destruction of much cultural heritage.

evidence: 1966: Red Guards attack the Four Olds.
From 1968: 'up to the mountains and down to the countryside'.

questions.label: Past paper: WHI02/1B, June 2025, Q4
questions.q: How significant were barefoot doctors in the development of health provision in China in the years 1949–76?

model.t: Barefoot doctors were significant in the development of health provision in China in 1949–76 because they took basic medicine to the countryside for the first time. However, the mass Patriotic Health Campaigns and the expansion of urban hospitals also mattered. Judged by scope and impact, barefoot doctors were the most significant development after 1965, but earlier campaigns did more to cut deaths from infectious disease.
model.n: Introduction: answers the question directly, names the other developments, sets criteria (scope, impact) and gives a qualified judgement.

model.t: Point: Barefoot doctors had very wide scope because they reached rural communes where most Chinese people lived.
model.n: P — topic sentence on the factor in the question, linked to a criterion.

model.t: Evidence: from 1965, after Mao attacked the Ministry of Health for serving only the cities, peasants were given a few months' training to give vaccinations, basic treatment and hygiene advice; by the mid-1970s there were well over a million of them.
model.n: E — precise, dated evidence (SPEDA: event, person, statistic). Check the figure against your class notes.

model.t: Explain: this meant that for the first time millions of villagers had regular access to some medical care, which helped raise life expectancy.
model.n: E — explains HOW the evidence shows significance.

model.t: Judge: however, their impact was limited by short training and shortages of medicine, so in terms of effectiveness they were less significant than the earlier campaigns against disease.
model.n: J — weighs the factor against a criterion (effectiveness) — this is what lifts the paragraph to Level 3–4.

model.t: Conclusion: Overall, barefoot doctors were highly significant in widening the scope of health provision after 1965, but the Patriotic Health Campaigns of the 1950s had a greater impact on reducing disease, so they were significant without being the single most important development across 1949–76.
model.n: Conclusion: ranks the developments against the criteria and covers the whole date range.

learn.intro: Emancipation freed about four million people. Reconstruction brought citizenship, the vote and black officeholders — and then a violent backlash and the federal government's retreat in 1877. Section B questions often compare this period with 1883–c1900 or 1933–45.

sections.title: 1. The Thirteenth Amendment and the realities of freedom

blocks.p: The Thirteenth Amendment (ratified December 1865) abolished slavery throughout the United States, except as punishment for a crime. About four million people were freed.

Economic position: freedpeople wanted land. General Sherman's Field Order No. 15 (January 1865) set aside coastal land in South Carolina and Georgia for black families, but President Andrew Johnson restored most confiscated land to former owners in 1865. Without land or capital, most freedpeople became wage labourers or sharecroppers — farming a landowner's land for a share of the crop — and the crop-lien system tied them to debt with local merchants.
Freedom of movement mattered enormously: people travelled to find family members separated by sale, moved to towns, and left plantations. Black churches became independent centres of community life.

Education: the Freedmen's Bureau (March 1865), northern missionary societies and black communities themselves set up schools; colleges such as Fisk (1866) and Howard (1867) were founded. Literacy was valued as a mark of freedom. White Southerners often met these changes with hostility and violence.

sections.title: 2. Johnson's response and the political settlement

blocks.p: Andrew Johnson, a Southern Democrat who became President after Lincoln's assassination in April 1865, offered lenient terms: pardons for most Confederates, and readmission once states abolished slavery and renounced secession. He showed no interest in black political rights.

Southern legislatures passed Black Codes (1865–66) — for example in Mississippi and South Carolina — controlling black workers through vagrancy laws, annual labour contracts and restrictions on property and movement. Johnson vetoed the renewal of the Freedmen's Bureau and the Civil Rights Act of 1866; Congress overrode him. Riots in Memphis and New Orleans in 1866 killed dozens of black people and turned northern opinion towards the Radical Republicans in the 1866 elections.

evidence: 1866: Civil Rights Act passed over Johnson's veto.

sections.title: 3. Radical Reconstruction, 1867–77

blocks.p: The Reconstruction Acts (1867) divided ten southern states into five military districts and required them to write new constitutions with black male suffrage and to ratify the Fourteenth Amendment before readmission. Johnson's opposition led to his impeachment (1868); he was acquitted by one vote.

The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) made all people born in the USA citizens and promised 'equal protection of the laws'. The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) banned denying the vote on grounds of 'race, color, or previous condition of servitude'. The Enforcement Acts (1870–71), including the Ku Klux Klan Act, let President Grant use federal force; in 1871 he suspended habeas corpus in parts of South Carolina. The Civil Rights Act of 1875 banned discrimination in public accommodations.

Black Americans held office in large numbers for the first time: Hiram Revels (1870) and Blanche K. Bruce (1875) of Mississippi sat in the US Senate, black representatives sat in Congress, and hundreds served in state legislatures. Their presence showed what political rights could achieve — and provoked fierce white resistance.

evidence: 1870: Fifteenth Amendment; Hiram Revels enters the Senate.

sections.title: 4. The backlash and the end of Reconstruction

blocks.p: The Ku Klux Klan, founded in Tennessee in 1865–66, used terror against black voters, officeholders, teachers and their white allies. After the Enforcement Acts weakened the Klan, paramilitary groups such as the White League in Louisiana (1874) and the Red Shirts acted openly. At Colfax, Louisiana (April 1873), dozens of black men were massacred after a disputed election.

Northern commitment faded: the economic depression after the Panic of 1873, corruption scandals and racism made voters tired of Reconstruction. The Supreme Court narrowed federal protection in the Slaughterhouse Cases (1873) and US v Cruikshank (1876). Democrats 'redeemed' one southern state after another, using violence and fraud, as in the 'Mississippi Plan' of 1875.

The disputed presidential election of 1876 was resolved by the Compromise of 1877: Republican Rutherford B. Hayes became President and the last federal troops were withdrawn from the South. Reconstruction ended, leaving the amendments on paper but black rights in the South largely unprotected.
