learn.intro: How could a few hundred Spanish soldiers bring down the Mexica (Aztec) Empire? And why did the Portuguese have such a different experience when Vasco da Gama entered the Indian Ocean? This topic compares two very different encounters.

sections.title: 1. The fall of the Mexica Empire

blocks.p: In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with roughly 500–600 Spanish soldiers. By 1521 the Mexica (Aztec) Empire, ruling millions from its capital Tenochtitlan, one of the largest cities in the world, had fallen. A small force defeating a huge empire needs several causes:

ul: ALLIANCES: many peoples resented Mexica rule. The Tlaxcalans, long-standing enemies of the Mexica, allied with Cortés and provided tens of thousands of warriors, arguably the biggest single factor.
DISEASE: smallpox devastated the Mexica, killing the emperor Cuitláhuac in 1520 at a critical moment.
TECHNOLOGY: steel weapons, some firearms and horses gave real but often overstated advantages.
POLITICS: Mexica caution and internal tensions gave Cortés time to build alliances.

blocks.p: Historians usually judge Indigenous alliances and disease the most significant. The popular idea that Spanish weapons alone won is a myth that erases the Indigenous allies who vastly outnumbered the Spanish.

evidence: Cortés landed in 1519 with about 500–600 soldiers.

blocks.p: In 1498 Vasco da Gama's fleet rounded Africa and reached Calicut on India's west coast, the first European ships to sail directly from Europe to India.

He did not arrive in an unconnected world. Calicut, ruled by the Zamorin, was part of the sophisticated Indian Ocean trading world. Da Gama's cheap trade goods did not impress, and established Arab merchants were rivals.

Because Portugal could not out-compete these merchants by trade alone, it turned to force: naval violence and fortified trading posts such as Hormuz (1507) and Goa (captured 1510) under Afonso de Albuquerque, to control key routes and tax trade.

The contrast matters: in the Indian Ocean, Europeans were one relatively weak newcomer trying to muscle into a powerful system. Portugal never controlled the whole of Indian Ocean trade, only parts of it, for a limited time.

learn.intro: Who gained and who lost from European expansion? This topic brings the unit together, introduces the transatlantic slave trade as a direct consequence of what you have studied, and asks who deserves to be remembered as a significant traveller, ready for your AP1 research project.

sections.title: 1. Who gained and who lost?

blocks.p: European expansion after 1492 had very different consequences for different groups:

ul: EUROPEAN POWERS gained enormously: silver and gold from the Americas (especially from Spanish mines at Potosí, from 1545), new crops and new colonies.
INDIGENOUS AMERICANS faced catastrophe: population collapse from disease, loss of land and independence, forced labour and conquest. They also survived, resisted and kept their cultures alive.

ENSLAVED AFRICANS: as Indigenous populations collapsed and European demand for labour on sugar plantations grew, Europeans turned to the forced transportation of enslaved people from West and Central Africa across the Atlantic. Over more than 300 years, over 12 million Africans were forcibly transported.

blocks.p: The transatlantic slave trade was directly connected to the processes you have studied: the Columbian Exchange, colonisation and plantation sugar.

"Winners and losers" can oversimplify. Not all Europeans gained (many ordinary sailors and soldiers died or gained little), and Indigenous and African peoples were not passive victims: they resisted, adapted and shaped outcomes.

evidence: Over 12 million Africans were forcibly transported across the Atlantic over more than 300 years.

sections.title: 2. Who changed the world? Judging significance

blocks.p: Significance is judged with criteria, not popularity: scale, impact, duration, revealing and remembered (the same toolkit you used in Year 7).

The criteria give surprising results. Zheng He's voyages were arguably larger in scale than Columbus's, but had less lasting global impact because China ended them. Columbus's first voyage was smaller, but its consequences, the Columbian Exchange and colonisation, were transformative and irreversible.
Significance also depends on whose perspective you take and which criteria you prioritise.

evidence: Criteria: scale, impact, duration, revealing, remembered.

sections.title: 3. Ready to research: your AP1 project

blocks.p: For AP1 you research one traveller or explorer and answer: How significant was your traveller's journey, and how should they be remembered?

Your planning sheet needs: the traveller and dates; your central argument; at least three credible sources with a bibliography; evidence about the route; motives; encounters; consequences; your chosen significance criteria; at least one alternative perspective; and an initial judgement.
Use credible sources (museums, universities, published historians) and record where each fact comes from.

topics.title: Why did Africans come to Tudor England?

review.note: Built from Mr Garry's own lessons for this unit (2026–27 scheme of work). Check wording against the lesson PowerPoints before relying on it.

learn.intro: Africans lived in England long before the 20th century. Historians have found hundreds of named Africans in Tudor and Stuart records, from royal trumpeters to sailors, divers and seamstresses. This topic asks why they came, using the push and pull factors that the Pearson GCSE Migrants in Britain course uses for every period.

sections.title: 1. An African presence in Tudor England

blocks.p: Africans lived in Tudor towns such as London, Southampton, Plymouth and Bristol. Miranda Kaufmann has documented over 360 named Africans in Britain between 1500 and 1640, and Onyeka Nubia argues that some were born in England.

Historians find them in parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials), royal accounts, court cases, letters and wills. Words used at the time included "blackamoore", "Moor" and "Ethiopian". These are historical terms, and they did not always mean the same thing.
This was part of England's growing international role: more trade, exploration and contact with Africa, Spain, Portugal and the Mediterranean.
Reasons were often mixed. Historians group them into push and pull factors:

ul: Royal and noble households: Catherine of Aragon arrived from Spain in 1501 with a household that included Africans. Spain and Portugal already had large African populations.
Trade: merchants traded with Morocco, West Africa and the Iberian peninsula. Mary Fillis came from Morocco around 1583.
Skills: Africans brought skills that were valued, such as music (John Blanke, trumpeter) and diving (Jacques Francis).
Escaping Spanish slavery: Diego escaped Spanish enslavement in Panama and joined Francis Drake in 1572.
Privateering: English ships attacked Spanish and Portuguese shipping, and Africans on board sometimes ended up in England.

blocks.p: Some came by choice, some were brought by others, and some escaped. A single person's journey could involve all three.

sections.title: 3. How historians know: Kaufmann and Onyeka

blocks.p: Two historians have shaped how we understand Black Tudors:

ul: Onyeka Nubia, "Blackamoores" (2013): argues Africans lived across urban England, were often employed for specialist skills, and were not automatically at the bottom of society.
Miranda Kaufmann, "Black Tudors" (2017): tells the stories of ten individuals, showing that Africans were baptised, married, paid wages and gave evidence in court.

blocks.p: Both use archives, but records only survive for some people, and are usually written by others. Asking whose voice survives is part of the history.

topics.title: Four Black Tudor lives: Blanke, Francis, Diego and Fillis

review.note: Built from Mr Garry's own lessons for this unit (2026–27 scheme of work). Check wording against the lesson PowerPoints before relying on it.

learn.intro: Four people, four very different journeys: a royal trumpeter, a salvage diver, a sailor who crossed the world with Drake, and a Moroccan woman who chose to be baptised in London. Their stories tell us a great deal about Tudor England.

blocks.p: John Blanke first appears in royal accounts in November 1507 as "John Blanke the blacke Trumpet", paid 8d a day, more than the standard 6d.
He may have arrived with Catherine of Aragon in 1501, but no record proves it. He played at Henry VII's funeral and Henry VIII's coronation in 1509.
He petitioned Henry VIII for a pay rise, asking for the post of a trumpeter who had died, Dominic Justinian. The king approved it.

He appears twice in the Westminster Tournament Roll of 1511, the only known portrait of a Black Tudor. In January 1512 Henry VIII gave him cloth for his wedding clothes, including violet cloth, a hat and a bonnet. After 1512 he disappears from the records.
Jacques Francis was born around 1527, probably on Arguin Island off Mauritania, West Africa, where diving skills were common.

He worked for Piero Paolo Corsi, a Venetian salvage contractor in Southampton, who called him his best diver. In 1546 Corsi's team was hired to recover guns from the wreck of the Mary Rose, which sank in 1545.

When Corsi was accused of stealing tin from another wreck, Francis gave evidence in the High Court of Admiralty on 8 February 1548, through an interpreter. He is the first known African to give evidence in an English court.
Opponents tried to dismiss him as a "slave" and an "infidel", but the court accepted his evidence. He called himself Corsi's "famulus", a servant, and evidence suggests he was paid.

sections.title: 3. Diego, circumnavigator

blocks.p: In 1572 Diego, who had escaped Spanish enslavement, ran through gunfire to reach Francis Drake's men at Nombre de Dios, Panama.
He helped the English ally with the Cimarrons, Africans who had escaped Spanish slavery, and together they captured a Spanish mule train carrying silver and gold.

He came to Plymouth with Drake and lived there for about four years. In November 1577 he sailed with Drake on the voyage around the world, serving as Drake's manservant and as an interpreter, since he spoke Spanish and English.

In November 1578 he was badly wounded by arrows on Mocha Island off Chile. He died of his wounds in 1579, near the Moluccas (Spice Islands). Evidence suggests he served under a contract, like other crew members.

evidence: Joined Drake 1572; sailed from Plymouth November 1577.

blocks.p: Mary Fillis was the daughter of Fillis of Morisco, a Moroccan basket weaver and shovel maker. She came to London around 1583, aged about six or seven.
She worked as a servant for John Barker, a merchant, and later for Millicent Porter, a seamstress in East Smithfield.

In 1597, around the age of 20, she asked to be baptised. The ceremony took place at St Botolph's, Aldgate. Choosing baptism suggests she wanted to belong to her community; it may also have helped her future.
She lived in London while Morocco and England were building an alliance against Spain. After Porter died in 1599, we do not know what happened to her.

topics.title: Free or enslaved? Status, experience and memory

review.note: Built from Mr Garry's own lessons for this unit (2026–27 scheme of work). Check wording against the lesson PowerPoints before relying on it.

learn.intro: Were Africans in Tudor England free or enslaved? What were their lives like? And did Elizabeth I really try to expel them? This topic weighs the evidence and the interpretations of historians.

blocks.p: English law in the 16th century did not clearly recognise slavery. The evidence suggests most Africans in Tudor England were treated as free people:

ul: They were paid wages (John Blanke, Jacques Francis, Diego).
They were baptised, married and buried in parish churches (Mary Fillis, John Blanke).
They could give evidence in court (Jacques Francis, 1548).

blocks.p: In the 1580s the Portuguese doctor Hector Nunes complained to the Court of Requests that an African man he had bought refused to serve him, and that he had no remedy under English common law. The Pearson GCSE Migrants course uses this petition as evidence about African freedom in Tudor England.

This did not mean equality. Africans usually worked as servants, and words like "blackamoore" could carry negative ideas. At the same time, Englishmen such as John Hawkins began slave-trading voyages from 1562, taking Africans to Spanish America, not England.

sections.title: 2. Experiences of everyday life

blocks.p: Black Tudors worked in many jobs: musicians, divers, sailors, servants, seamstresses and silk weavers. Onyeka argues many were employed for specialist skills; Kaufmann shows them in households from the royal court to villages.
Many were baptised and married English partners, which suggests they were part of local communities rather than separate from them. Others, like Diego, lived mobile lives at sea.
Experiences varied by class, gender, job and place, just as they did for other Tudor people.

evidence: Jobs: musicians, divers, sailors, servants, seamstresses, silk weavers.

blocks.p: On 18 July 1596 the Privy Council issued an open letter allowing Caspar van Senden, a merchant from Lübeck, to take "Blackamoores" from England to Spain and Portugal, but only with their masters' consent.
Masters refused, so van Senden got nothing. A harsher draft proclamation from 1601 survives among Robert Cecil's papers, but it was never issued.

Kaufmann argues this was a failed business deal with one merchant, not a deportation, and Africans stayed in England. The claim that "Elizabeth I expelled all Black people" is a myth that was repeated for years.
How we remember Black Tudors matters. Their stories show that Black British history did not begin in the 20th century.

topics.title: When does change become a revolution? Why Britain?

review.note: Built from Mr Garry's own lessons for this unit (2026–27 scheme of work). Check wording against the lesson PowerPoints before relying on it.

learn.intro: Britain in 1750 was mostly rural; by 1900 it was the world's first industrialised, majority-urban nation. But calling this a "revolution" is a historian's judgement, not a fact. This topic gives you the tools to judge it (Scale, Speed, Depth, Duration) and asks why industrialisation began in Britain.

sections.title: 1. Change, continuity and revolution

blocks.p: In 1750 roughly three-quarters of people worked on the land, most goods were made by hand in homes or small workshops, and travel was slow and local. By 1900 most people worked in industry and lived in towns, and railways crossed the country in hours. England's population grew from around 6 million in 1750 to over 30 million by 1900.
The phrase "Industrial Revolution" was popularised by historians looking back, notably Arnold Toynbee in the 1880s. It is a later label and an argument that needs evidence.

Judge with the four criteria: Scale (how many people), Speed (how quickly), Depth (how fundamentally lives changed), Duration (how lasting). You will track every development in the unit against these criteria in your Revolution Tracker.
Two traps: change is not the same as progress (it can make things worse for some people), and "revolutionary" does not mean "positive".

evidence: England: about 6 million people in 1750; over 30 million by 1900.

sections.title: 2. Why Britain?

blocks.p: Historians reject a single cause in favour of interconnected causes, a "perfect storm":

ul: Agriculture: more food meant fewer farm workers were needed, freeing labour for industry.
Population: England's population roughly doubled during the 18th century, supplying workers and consumers.
Coal: large, accessible reserves powered steam engines and furnaces.
Capital: money from farming, banking, merchant trade and Atlantic and colonial trade, including trade linked to the enslavement of Africans (explored in the next topic).
Transport: turnpike roads and canals from the 1760s (the Bridgewater Canal opened in 1761) moved goods cheaply.
Institutions: stable government, secure property rights and patent law gave inventors and investors confidence.

blocks.p: Older stories credited a few "great inventors". Historians now stress how these causes reinforced each other.

evidence: Causes were interconnected, not a list.

learn.intro: How far was Britain's Industrial Revolution built on the world beyond Britain? And how revolutionary was the Agricultural Revolution that came before it? This topic follows cotton from enslaved labour in the Americas to Lancashire's mills, then returns to the English countryside.

sections.title: 1. The revolution behind the revolution

blocks.p: A chain connected Britain's industry to the wider world:

ul: Enslaved Africans were forced to grow raw cotton on plantations in the Americas.
Cotton was shipped through British ports such as Liverpool, Bristol and Glasgow, which grew rich on Atlantic trade.
It was processed into cloth in Lancashire's mills.
Finished cloth was sold in Britain, Europe and colonial and global markets, generating profits that could be reinvested.

blocks.p: Profits linked to the slave trade and colonial trade also fed banking, insurance and infrastructure in port cities.

This is a genuine debate. The historian Eric Williams argued in "Capitalism and Slavery" (1944) that profits from slavery were a crucial engine of British industrial capital. Other historians argue those profits were too small a share of total investment to be the main cause. The most defensible position is that global and domestic factors were interconnected: mills needed slave-grown cotton AND British capital, coal, machines and workers.

evidence: Liverpool, Bristol and Glasgow grew rich on Atlantic trade.

blocks.p: Before enclosure, much land was farmed in open strips shared by a village, with common land for grazing and fuel. Enclosure fenced it into larger private fields. Enclosure Acts were especially numerous from the 1760s to the 1830s.

ul: Jethro Tull's seed drill (1701) sowed seed in straight rows, using seed more efficiently than scattering by hand.
Viscount "Turnip" Townshend popularised four-field crop rotation (wheat, turnips, barley, clover), keeping soil fertile without leaving fields fallow, and providing winter animal feed.
Robert Bakewell's selective breeding produced larger, faster-maturing sheep and cattle.

blocks.p: Food production rose, supporting a growing population and freeing workers for industry. But enclosure caused real hardship: smallholders and labourers lost rights to common land, pushing some into poverty, wage labour or migration to towns. A landowner and a labourer might disagree about whether this was a "revolution", or progress.

timeline.event: Robert Bakewell develops selective breeding; Enclosure Acts multiply.
Slavery is abolished in most of the British Empire.

learn.intro: The Spinning Jenny, the Water Frame, the power loom and the steam engine moved work from homes into factories, and people from villages into fast-growing cities. Did machines change lives more than anything else? And did industrialisation transform life for everyone?

sections.title: 1. From hand to machine

ul: James Hargreaves' Spinning Jenny (in use from the mid-1760s, patented 1770) let one worker spin several threads at once.
Richard Arkwright's Water Frame (1769) used water power to spin stronger thread. It needed a mill by a river: Cromford Mill (1771) was one of the first true factories.
Edmund Cartwright's power loom (1785) mechanised weaving, but was unreliable at first and took decades to spread: mechanisation was gradual.
James Watt's improved steam engine (patented 1769, refined in the 1770s–80s) freed factories from rivers, so industry grew in coalfield towns.

blocks.p: The factory system mattered as much as the machines. Under the "domestic" or "putting-out" system, people worked at home at their own pace. In factories, machines, clocks, bells and fines set the pace. Some workers earned more, but many lost control over their working lives.

evidence: Water Frame 1769; Cromford Mill 1771; power loom 1785.

blocks.p: Manchester grew from around 18,000 people in the 1750s to over 300,000 by 1850, driven by cotton.
Push factors (low farm wages, loss of common land after enclosure) and pull factors (factory jobs, often higher wages) drove migration to towns.
Growth was unplanned. Working-class families often lived in overcrowded back-to-back houses, sharing an outdoor toilet with many others, with no running water or rubbish removal.

Experience depended on class. Middle-class factory owners, merchants and professionals lived in larger homes, enjoyed new shops, theatres and parks, and sometimes moved to suburbs away from pollution. There was no single experience of "the industrial city".

learn.intro: How revolutionary was industrialisation for children? And how successfully did Britain respond to the filth and disease it created? This topic uses real evidence about child labour, evaluates Oliver! as a later interpretation, and follows the public health reformers.

sections.title: 1. A child's revolution

blocks.p: Children worked long hours, often 12–14 hours a day, six days a week. In mills they pieced broken threads or crawled under machinery to clear blockages; in mines they worked as "trappers" opening ventilation doors or hauled coal tubs. Accidents from exhaustion and unguarded machines were common.
For many working-class families, children's wages were essential household income. That is context, not an excuse.

Government inquiries such as the Sadler Committee (1832) collected testimony from child workers. They are a key source, but were gathered to support reform, so historians read them with that purpose in mind.

Reform was gradual: the 1833 Factory Act limited children's hours and set minimum ages in textile mills (enforcement was patchy), and the 1842 Mines Act banned underground work for women and children under 10.

Oliver! (1968 film, based on Dickens's 1838 novel Oliver Twist) is a later interpretation, not evidence. It shows a workhouse and London pickpockets, not factory or mine work, so it blurs different experiences of poverty.

evidence: Sadler Committee 1832; Factory Act 1833; Mines Act 1842.
Oliver! (1968) is an interpretation, not evidence.

blocks.p: Industrial towns grew faster than any planning: no piped water, no sewage removal, a few outdoor toilets for dozens of families. Cholera, a waterborne disease, caused major epidemics in 1831–32, 1848–49 and 1854, killing tens of thousands.

ul: Edwin Chadwick's 1842 report used statistics to argue that poor sanitation caused disease and cost money. It helped lead to the 1848 Public Health Act, the first significant national public health law.
John Snow's 1854 investigation in Soho mapped cholera cases to the Broad Street water pump, evidence that cholera spread through water, not "bad air" (miasma). It took years to be accepted.
Joseph Bazalgette designed London's sewer network, built mainly in the 1860s after the "Great Stink" of 1858.

blocks.p: The response was gradual and contested. Many feared government interference and the cost, so change came slowly and unevenly. Did industrialisation solve the problems it created, or did government action?

learn.intro: Time to judge. This topic brings the whole unit together with the Revolution Tracker, prepares you for the Harkness debate, then applies the same criteria to the Internet and to AI, including what the Industrial Revolution can teach us about the UAE's future.

sections.title: 1. Was it really a revolution?

blocks.p: Use the four criteria (Scale, Speed, Depth, Duration) to compare very different changes fairly. Change that looks dramatic on one criterion can look less revolutionary on another:

ul: Urbanisation scores very high on Scale (millions moved) but more moderately on Speed within one town (growth over decades).
A single invention such as the power loom had narrow immediate Scale but very high Depth for the workers it replaced.
Agricultural change was slower, but it was a precondition for everything else.

blocks.p: Not every area of life changed equally. Some things showed continuity, such as the monarchy, many rural ways of life and religious practice. A strong judgement shows this unevenness rather than claiming "everything changed".

evidence: Compare developments on all four criteria, not just one.

blocks.p: Assessment proposition: "The Industrial Revolution changed the world more profoundly than the revolutions that followed it." How far do you agree?

A Harkness discussion is student-led and evidence-based. The teacher observes. You are marked on Knowledge, Precise evidence, Historical reasoning, Responding/building/challenging, and a short written Final judgement (4 marks each, 20 in total).
Prepare an Evidence Bank: your three strongest pieces of evidence, one counterargument to your own view, and two questions to ask classmates. Do not script a speech.

ul: Build: "Building on what X said…"
Challenge: "I would challenge that because…"
Agree with nuance: "I agree to some extent, but the evidence from… suggests…"
Question: "What evidence supports that claim?"

sections.title: 3. From steam to silicon: the Internet and AI

blocks.p: Key milestones: ARPANET sent the first message between computers in 1969; Tim Berners-Lee's World Wide Web became publicly available in 1991, making the Internet usable by non-specialists; e-commerce, search and social media spread from the mid-1990s; the smartphone era (often dated from the iPhone in 2007) made constant mobile access normal for billions.
Compare with the criteria: the Internet spread globally in roughly 20–30 years (Speed) to billions (Scale). Its Depth is huge, but its Duration cannot yet be judged with hindsight.
Mechanisation mainly replaced physical tasks; automation and AI increasingly perform cognitive tasks too, a significant difference.

The UAE is pursuing rapid economic and technological change, diversifying beyond oil and investing in education, innovation and AI, while emphasising heritage, community and national identity. History teaches caution: people in 1750 could not predict 1900, so we should be careful about confident predictions about AI.

model.t: The Industrial Revolution changed the world considerably more profoundly than later revolutions, to a large extent, because its depth of change was unmatched.

It transformed where people lived and how they worked: Manchester grew from around 18,000 people in the 1750s to over 300,000 by 1850, and new public health laws such as the 1848 Act changed the relationship between government and citizens.
However, the Internet and AI may prove faster and larger in scale, even if their depth and duration cannot yet be judged with hindsight.
Therefore the Industrial Revolution's profundity lies in its depth and its now-provable duration, an advantage later, still-unfolding revolutions cannot yet claim.

learn.intro: Why did Europe go to war in 1914? Historians usually start with four long-term causes, remembered as M.A.I.N.: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism and Nationalism. Each built tension over decades. Your job is to explain how they linked, and to judge which mattered most.

blocks.p: Militarism is the belief that a country should build up strong armed forces and be ready to use them. The Great Powers spent heavily on armies and navies before 1914.

ul: The naval race: Germany's Navy Laws (1898 and 1900) aimed to build a fleet to rival Britain's. Britain launched HMS Dreadnought in 1906, a battleship so advanced it made older ships out of date, and both countries raced to build more. In 1909 the British public demanded "We want eight and we won't wait".
Huge armies: France, Germany, Russia and Austria-Hungary relied on conscription, so millions of men could be mobilised quickly.

War plans: Germany's Schlieffen Plan (drawn up around 1905) planned to defeat France quickly by going through Belgium before turning on Russia. Plans like this meant that once mobilisation started, it was hard to stop.

blocks.p: Militarism increased fear and suspicion, and it made generals' timetables part of political decisions in July 1914.

sections.title: 2. Alliances

blocks.p: By 1914 Europe was divided into two armed camps:

ul: The Triple Alliance (1882): Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy.
The Triple Entente: France and Russia allied in 1894; Britain and France signed the Entente Cordiale in 1904; Britain and Russia reached agreement in 1907.

blocks.p: Alliances were meant to deter attack, but they could turn a local quarrel into a wider war, because a conflict involving one member could pull in its partners. Britain's ententes were friendly understandings rather than firm promises to fight; Britain's decision in August 1914 was strongly shaped by Germany invading Belgium, whose neutrality Britain had guaranteed in the Treaty of London (1839).
Italy did not join its allies in 1914, and entered the war in 1915 on the Entente side. That shows alliances did not automatically decide what countries did.

evidence: Franco-Russian Alliance 1894; Entente Cordiale 1904; Anglo-Russian Entente 1907.

blocks.p: Imperialism is when a powerful country builds an empire by taking control of other lands. By 1914 Britain had the largest empire in the world, and France also had a vast empire.

In the "Scramble for Africa", European powers divided almost the whole continent between them, agreeing rules at the Berlin Conference (1884–85). Africans resisted, but by 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.

Germany, united only in 1871, wanted its own empire. Under Kaiser Wilhelm II's Weltpolitik ("world policy"), it demanded "a place in the sun". Rivalry over Morocco led to two crises, in 1905 (Tangier) and 1911 (Agadir). Both times Britain backed France, which brought them closer and increased German fears of being "encircled".

sections.title: 4. Nationalism

blocks.p: Nationalism is a strong pride in your nation, and often the belief that each nation should rule itself.

ul: In the Balkans, Serbian nationalists wanted to unite South Slav peoples, including those ruled by Austria-Hungary. Russia supported Slavs (Pan-Slavism).
In 1908 Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina, angering Serbia and Russia (the Bosnian Crisis).
The Balkan Wars (1912–13) made Serbia larger and more confident, alarming Austria-Hungary.
The Black Hand, a secret Serbian nationalist society founded in 1911, used violence to pursue its aims.
In France, many wanted to recover Alsace-Lorraine, lost to Germany in 1871.

blocks.p: Nationalism also meant that, in 1914, many people in every country supported going to war.

evidence: Bosnian Crisis 1908; Balkan Wars 1912–13; Black Hand founded 1911.

model.t: Militarism was a highly important long-term cause, but to a large extent it mattered because of the alliance system.

The naval race, from Germany's Navy Laws of 1898 and 1900 to HMS Dreadnought in 1906, made Britain see Germany as a threat, and the Schlieffen Plan meant a war with Russia would also be a war with France through Belgium.
This meant that once mobilisation began in July 1914, military timetables and alliance commitments turned a Balkan crisis into a European war.
Therefore militarism was not the main cause on its own; it was most dangerous when combined with alliances and Balkan nationalism.

learn.intro: On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand was shot in Sarajevo. Within six weeks the Great Powers were at war. This topic follows the July Crisis step by step and asks how the trigger set off the long-term causes.

blocks.p: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, visited Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia, with his wife Sophie on 28 June 1914.

A group of young Bosnian Serb nationalists, armed with help from the Black Hand, planned to kill him. A bomb attack that morning failed. Later, after the archduke's car took a wrong turn, Gavrilo Princip shot Franz Ferdinand and Sophie dead.
Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and saw a chance to crush Serbian nationalism.

sections.title: 2. The July Crisis

blocks.p: Step by step, the crisis spread:

ul: 5–6 July: Germany gives Austria-Hungary the "blank cheque", promising support whatever it does.
23 July: Austria-Hungary sends Serbia an ultimatum with harsh demands.
28 July: Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia.
30 July: Russia orders general mobilisation to support Serbia.
1 August: Germany declares war on Russia.
3 August: Germany declares war on France.
4 August: Germany invades Belgium (the Schlieffen Plan); Britain declares war on Germany.

blocks.p: The trigger was the assassination, but the long-term causes explain why a murder in the Balkans became a world war: nationalism created the crisis, alliances and the blank cheque widened it, and militarism (mobilisation timetables and the Schlieffen Plan) made it hard to stop. Remember Alphonse the Camel: the final straw was not the only reason for the collapse.

evidence: Blank cheque 5–6 July; ultimatum 23 July; Britain declares war 4 August 1914.
